Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct a question to the government, and I should like to have the attention of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. My question is based on a report appearing in the western press. I quote from the Leader-Post, of Regina, dated May 3, under the heading "Farmers assured good crop prices under proposal in United States":
Washington, May 3.-The United States agricultural department laid before farm leaders in and out of congress Friday a broad legislative proposal which would assure farmers cooperating with this year's federal crop programme $1.04 a bushel for wheat and 78-8 cents for corn.
These returns compare with present receipts of about 83 cents for wheat and 75 cents for corn. In both cases the figures are averages, and government benefit payments, at present rates, are included.
New loans would be made at 75 per cent of parity for basic crops-wheat, cotton, et cetera. At present loan rates are about 56 per cent of parity for cotton and wheat. (Parity is a term used to describe crop prices which would give farm commodities purchasing power, in terms of non-farm goods and services, equal to that which they possessed in some past period, usually the years 1910-14).
Under the department's proposal, the commodity loan rates would be increased from 66 cents to 85 cents for wheat.
This is the announcement I referred to as coming when I spoke the other day. My question is this, Mr. Speaker. Will the government, in view of this announcement by the United States government, now reconsider its 1941 wheat marketing policy and set a fair parity price, net, to the Canadian wheat farmer comparable with the price, net, set to the United States farmer according to this announcement? If the government is not prepared to answer to-day, will it agree to take my question under consideration and give an answer perhaps to-morrow?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry to have to prolong the debate on the matter raised by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), but I consider it to be of sufficient importance to hon. members to express briefly an opinion on the question, as I see and understand the government's proposal to discontinue direct relief.
During his discussion of the matter, the hon. member for Weyburn pointed, out to the house that in November, 1940, the last date on which figures are available, the number of people on direct relief was approximately 250,500. That in itself, in my opinion, should give hon. members cause for reflection. At that time there was that large number of citizens of this country who, in order to eke out an existence, depended on the federal government's contribution to assist the provinces to carry out their relief schedules or schemes. I am particularly interested in the question as it pertains to the province from which I come and with whose situation I am familiar.
On checking over the figures, I find that the returns for Nova Scotia as of October, 1939. listed heads of families on relief as 958, the total number including dependents being 4,573. The figures contained in the report of November, 1940. show heads of families on relief in Nova Scotia as 228, the total number on relief at that time being 898. For purposes

Sup-ply-Unemployment
of comparison between 1939 and 1940, the figures are misleading. In checking them over one would be led to believe that there has been an increase of employment, and that relief has automatically dropped off because of that fact. I know that that is not true.
Another thing in that connection with which I am concerned is that every province with the exception of Nova Scotia has made a declaration of where it stands in this matter. British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Ontario and other provinces have stated that they are prepared to carry that burden to the extent of, in some cases, 75 per cent. In our province there has been no declaration from the government as to whether they are going to make any contribution to relief, and I know that in many of the towns and municipalities there is an urgent need of the continuation of direct relief until such a time as the recipients of it shall have been absorbed into employment.
The figures are misleading when compared with those of 1939 and 1940. For October, 1939, they are as I have given them. The reason for the apparent decline in the number of those receiving relief in Nova Scotia is that the provincial government has discontinued direct relief in any town, city or municipality where there is not five per cent of the total population totally unemployed. Under that regulation hundreds of people who were and should be receiving relief have become a charge upon the municipality or the city or town. These bodies have been obliged to assume the total cost of issuing relief and as a result the recipients have disappeared from the statistics compiled by the federal government.
Let me give a few examples. Last session I read into the record a resolution from the town of New Waterford complaining of the very thing I am trying to put before the house at the present moment. Owing to the fact that the provincial government had discontinued relief in that town because there was not five per cent of the total population totally unemployed, the citizens were petitioning the federal government for some action looking to the alleviation of the distress in the town. That resolution stated that there were at that time 350 men unemployed in the town of New Waterford, that there was no prospect of their obtaining employment, and so forth. Notwithstanding that these 350 men would be qualified for relief under the conditions obtaining in the rest of Canada, that town was obliged to accept the responsibility one hundred per cent of caring for them. But these men do not appear in the statistics for 1940 as compiled by the federal government. Relief in that town was discontinued by the provincial government in February, 1938, and the town has been 14873-163
struggling to take care of its own unemployment problem. It has meant for the town a burden which it is not very well able to carry.
When the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) announced that relief was to be discontinued on a certain date I made it my business to get in contact with some of the larger towns in my province, particularly in my own end of the province. I received a telegram from the mayor of Glace Bay, where relief is quite serious. It was dated February 19 and in it he stated that the present weekly disbursements amount to approximately SS00. The other facts he indicated were that there were 100 heads of families, 50 single, no home connections, involving in all approximately 500 dependents, 50 employable in industry if employment could be found. For the rest the town would assume responsibility if the government would find employment for others who were on relief at that time.
In the city of Sydney relief has been discontinued since the provincial government made the stipulation with respect to the five per cent. The mayor of the city sent me this telegram on March 8:
No direct relief received by Sydney for two years. Provincial government insists five per cent population unemployed before relief given. Sydney spent $35,000 last year on relief. Drain too heavy for the city. Urge federal government supply total relief but not to able bodied men alone. Large number undernourished men on relief employers will not employ.
That is the situation in Sydney. These were men not registered with the steel company for employment. In this last month approximately 1,600 able-bodied young men were seeking employment. That city has been endeavouring for the past two years to care for its own unemployment situation, and while the war has absorbed a small percentage of the men, the city has still a serious unemployment problem on its hands.
I take these few telegrams merely as examples of the general situation throughout that end of the country. Take the town of Reserve Mines. I have been checking up on the facts in that town. One of its mines closed recently, and that means that there is an additional unemployment problem. That particular town is not getting its taxes-probably about forty per cent of them. The school teachers have not been paid for four months because the town is not able to collect the necessary taxes to pay them. The teachers were threatening a strike because their salaries had been four months in arrears, but some temporary arrangement has been made in that on that question. There is, however, a serious unemployment problem there, affecting the

Supply-Unemployment

life of the whole community, even to the extent of disrupting the educational system.
I know that the people in charge of affairs in that particular municipal council cannot meet relief requirements, and the same is true generally. In Thorburn on the mainland of Nova Scotia there are approximately 1,200 people. It is a relief camp. These people depend absolutely on relief and owing to the action of the government in discontinuing direct relief they are now without any means whatever. Nothing will be done for them. A large percentage of people there are unemployed through no fault of their own and cannot obtain work.
Perhaps the men in the different governing bodies who have studied the question have been misled by the statistics as compiled. As I read them they would lead one to believe that there has been a sufficient decrease in the unemployment relief rolls throughout Canada to warrant the action that has been taken, but I have given examples to show how these figures can mislead. It is not that the necessity for relief has disappeared; the fact is that the provincial governments have ceased to issue relief and have relegated past recipients of relief to the ranks of pauperism, to work out their own problems for themselves.
During the recess I had meetings with a large group of men in the town of Glace Bay, heads of families cut off at a moment's notice. They were appealing to some one to find a way out of the difficulty. They appealed to the provincial government. The tdwn has carried them as far as it can, and their families are dependent upon relief. These men have been trying to get into the army but they have not succeeded and they cannot get any work. So that until that situation is met completely to the satisfaction of those who are concerned about it, the government's action in discontinuing relief should be reconsidered.
There are thousands of people who depend absolutely upon relief for their livelihood. As pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), the cost to the government for the last year was thirteen and a quarter million dollars. After listening here to people talking about billions during the past year I have begun to look upon thirteen millions as small change.
If we can spend millions of dollars to prosecute the war, which is necessary at this time, and if we are to maintain and extend democracy, then there is no justification for the present condition. The first consideration is the need of the people within the framework of the democracy that we talk so much about. It is not an inspiring sight to see young men coming from different parts of

Canada billeted in towns and cities and hundreds of men and women seeking relief and not able to get it. The first question I would ask under similar circumstances is, is this the democracy I am going to fight for? I find the governing bodies of the country unmindful of the needs of the people to the extent that they are left milling around in the middle of the road without direction; is that the democracy I am going to fight for? It does not tend to encourage recruiting.
The whole thing is a relatively small matter and one that should be handled carefully until, as pointed out by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Munitions and Supply, within the next six months or a year there is a shortage of labour and we may be able to utilize these unemployed people and give them a chance to work; for work is the solution of our problem. Until they are absorbed in some gainful occupation and made self-supporting, relief should be continued.
I have no intention of delaying the house with matters that perhaps others consider less important. But I wanted to make these few remarks because I think that this discontinuance of relief, and this refusal of provincial governments to accept responsibility, thus throwing it upon towns and municipalities which are bankrupt through taking care of the problem during the past ten years, is a matter that should not be handled as it is being handled at present. It reflects on the judgment of those in authority; it is anything but inspiring and it is a condition which should be remedied at once.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I intend to take just a few moments to discuss this matter and to voice most strongly my protest against the situation that exists in this country in respect of unemployment and relief. My protest is that the federal government has saddled the entire responsibility of relief upon the provinces, something which at this particular time they could ill afford to do. I do not know how each of the nine provincial governments is handling this added burden. Some of them may be passing it on to the municipalities; others may be striking a happy medium with the municipalities, while still others may be taking up the entire burden that the federal government has thrown upon them. I know that the Alberta government has assumed the entire burden. It is not passing the burden on to the municipalities.
The very moment that the federal government handed this burden on to the provinces the reaction was that some municipalities took advantage of the action of the government by intimating to the public that there

Supply-Unemployment
was no further need for unemployment relief, and immediately cut families off their own relief lists. That is absolutely unfair. People must be cared for if they are unable to care for themselves. This action has led to a good deal of dissension and dissatisfaction. If we want to maintain a measure of contentment in this country and full cooperation in the war effort, it ill behooves any municipality to act in such a manner.
I strongly protest against the situation as it exists. I protest against the fact that we have any unemployment and relief in Canada at all, after nearly two years of war. The present government came into office in 1935. In that year nazism was becoming a glaring danger to the democratic countries of the world; yet after almost six years of administration by the same government and nearly two years of war, we still have to discuss in this house, as matters of national importance, unemployment and relief. The problem still remains. I was out west some few weeks ago, during the Easter recess, and had occasion to observe the situation in some measure. I discovered there were certain types of individuals, of certain ages, certain groups of people, who were cut off relief, who wanted to find employment but could not find it. I know this is only a small part of the whole national situation, but I have reference, for instance, to mining communities. If they are all like the one in my constituency the situation is this: that during recent years when the coal mining sections were running part time-now of course they are running a little better, perhaps nearly full time

many of the miners reached the age of sixty or sixty-five, and they are now told that they are too old to work. But they are too young to get the old age pension, and there is no relief for them. If this country is trying to attain a total war effort, there should be some place in our national war effort where those men could be usefully employed and enabled to keep the wolf from the door.
It has been brought to my attention also that there are other types of people who were on relief and have been cut off on the pretence that the dominion government has done this because psychologically at least there should no longer be unemployment and relief. I have reference to widows with families, who have to live on the barest necessities because there is no relief for them.
I am not going to prolong the debate, but I protest against the fact that there should be about a quarter of a million people in this country either on relief or unemployed when we are supposed to be engaged in a total war effort. It is really a shame. I believe hon. members of this group are with me in saying that we strongly protest against that condition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like the indulgence of the house for just a few moments in order to refer to an article which appeared in Life magazine under date of May 5, and to make a protest with regard to one paragraph contained in that article, which was written by one Eliot Janeway, an associate editor of Time magazine, under the heading "Roosevelt vs. Hitler." The paragraph is as follows:
Canada, on the other hand, has not yet begun to integrate with Roosevelt's new order and Roosevelt has not been needling her. Toronto greeted Willkie enthusiastically. Yet the timid, unimaginative Mackenzie King government continues to be blackmailed by the crudely proAxis French Canadian minority (an ideal nazi fifth column). The war has boomed Canada's economy, and made her a liaison between the U.S. and England. Yet all Mackenzie King wants to talk to the U.S. about is munitions financing. And he has dared only to raise Canada's original one-month conscription term to a scarcely less absurd four months. King and Churchill are not close, although King and Roosevelt are. (They are both Harvard men.) This accounts for the most promising step about to be taken toward Canadian-U.S. integration; the beginning of Roosevelt's favourite St. Lawrence seaway, which will in a few years embrace big sections of both countries in a unified regional structure comparable to TVA. Meanwhile, leadership is needed, and only Roosevelt can provide it, if he will. Ottawa's job is to declare independence from the axis transmission belt in French Quebec.
I am an English-speaking resident of the province of Quebec; I represent a county of that province, and I protest with all the force at my command against this reference to the people of my province whose language is French. Those people are just as patriotic and loyal as any Canadians in this parliament or anywhere else, and they should not be slandered in this way. I would ask that someone in authority take up this matter.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not ban the magazine?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would agree to that, if it were possible, but I do think this matter should be taken up. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) can defend himself; the members of the government can defend themselves, but I do not think this slander against the province of Quebec should be allowed to pass.
I remember that at the opening of this session two very popular members of this house, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) made reference to the loyalty and patriotism of what they called the French-Canadians. I prefer to call them Canadians whose language is French, because we are all Canadians. I appreciate the statements of those two hon. gentlemen, because I do not
Supply-Unemployment

think anyone in this parliament knows the people of Quebec whose language is French better than I do. I know them inside out and outside in; I have been associated with them all my life, and I claim that they have just as much patriotism as any other group of Canadians. I think it is a shame that any reference of this kind should be made to them.
It is often said that the Roman Catholics of Quebec obey, their clergy. No doubt when that is said it is meant that they obey the cardinal of the Roman Catholic church. I should like to read a statement made in Toronto on April 17 by Cardinal Villeneuve, who said:
There is far down within us something deeper than personal interests, than personal kinships, than party feeling; it is the need and the will to be of service to our country and that will is rightly termed patriotism. . . .
We are fighting for ideals which are imponderable; ideals which cannot be measured, weighed and calculated, but are priceless; righteousness, honour, peace, freedom, ideals which cannot but be pleasing to God. And we may confidently leave their triumph in His almighty hands.
Last year, at a religious demonstration _ in Quebec City, the cardinal voiced his opinion of Hitler in terms which leave no room for doubt as to the Catholic attitude towards the German reich:
As a persecuting and sacrilegious potentate, murderer of women and children, Hitler represents the felony and the very organization of evil. His adversaries and victims represent patriotism and right.
The premier of the province of Quebec is one of the finest gentlemen ever to occupy that position. I am going to read what he said to his people, and to ask if anyone then will say that the people of my province are not loyal and patriotic:
"Our sons," he told the Canadian Club of Montreal, "have risen for the defence of Canada. They have crossed the seas to succour threatened Great Britain, which has become the first bulwark of Christianity, liberty and honour. . . . No one refused to serve when national registration was called, no one refuses to help when war loans and other corollary works are organized; no one questions the justice of the cause, or holds back on the effort."
Later the premier emphasized Quebec's position in the following terms:
We are accomplishing our duty, our full duty in close formation with the other provinces and the central government. We are conscious of being among those who work with fervour, constancy and practical sense for the realization of the ideal of Canadian national unity.
Is that not sufficient proof that the leader of the Roman Catholic church in Quebec and the premier of that province are behind this government in its all-out war effort? Surely there can be no doubt about it. I do hope

this matter will be taken up with the United States minister and a protest made against this article, whose author should have known better than to write the paragraph I have quoted.
Now I should like to say a word in regard to what the people of Quebec think about this government and why they support it. Quebec has confidence in the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and I am sure every hon. member of this house will agree that these two hon. gentlemen are great Canadians. We may not agree with everything that is being done, but we must agree that on the whole the Prime Minister and his government are carrying on a gigantic undertaking in a very satisfactory manner, and that they are keeping the members of the house continually informed as to what is being done. I make this statement in order to put in clear language exactly why we in Quebec support the Liberal government. It is not just a matter of politics; we believe this is the best government this country could have at the present time. There is no doubt at all about that. I believe the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice will go down ini history as two of the greatest Canadians this country has ever known.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
during no time in the history of Canada did the common man, the labourer or the youth of this nation decay more rapidly than under the rotten system of relief forced upon the people of this country.
What is relief? It seems to me it is a natural consequence of the change in the economic and industrial life which has taken place throughout the world. It is the result of a changed economy in which machinery has replaced the labourer, and production can take place with reduced manual labour. Naturally many people have been thrown out of work.
Canada is a nation of about 11,000,000 people who occupy the north half of the richest continent in the world. Canada has more wealth, resources, food and everything man requires, than have the people of any other nation. The United States is a nation of 130,000,000 people living in the southern half of the same continent. But they have been able to arrange for their people a fairly decent standard of living-or at least 100,000,000 of them. Only a few years ago we in Canada sent over a million people to our relief rolls. I do not know that there can be anything more deteriorating than that the youth of our nation and others who want to work, who are willing to do almost anything to keep their homes together, should be denied the right of exchanging their labour for a decent living.
I condemn the government for not having made a decent analysis of the problem, for not having found the causes, for not taking any decent, constructive attitude toward a condition which has tended to ruin the nation. To-day we are reaping some of the results of the degeneration which took place since 1935, and even before that time. For centuries man laboured to save himself from starvation. People starved because they did not know how to produce sufficient food, clothing and shelter to keep themselves supplied. But since the industrial revolution, since the advancement of science, much progress has been made, and we have now reached the point where a man has been able to produce far more than he can consume. We are smothered in a load of abundance which leaves us starving.
We now have to take money from the taxpayers to pay bonuses to the farmers on the prairies so that they will not produce food. At the same time in some of the cities and even in rural parts of the very same country we find people who are hungry and in need. It would seem to me that after centuries of struggle, man, suddenly reaching the goal toward which he had struggled so many years, that of having gained power
over the resources of nature, finds that the cup has been dashed from his lips and that he is left in a state of want, poverty and degeneration.
Now when our young men go up for medical attention they find they cannot pass the physical examinations. Why? They have endured too much hardship. There has been too much riding on box cars, too much begging from door to door, insufficient food, improper nourishment, lack of medical and dental care. The medical records of the military authorities are a disgrace and a blot on Canada's record. The blame is to be placed on governments of this country which have refused to face the facts in a decent and scientific way and have had no constructive policy to place before the people. The degeneration has seeped right into the very homes, the foundation and core of a nation. It is because of those homes that Canada is failing to-day.
Now with a war upon us and with thousands of people still on relief the government refuses to continue to grant even that little crust of bread needed to keep body and soul together. I do not know what the government is going to do about this matter, but if it does not begin doing something at this time to cure unemployment, eradicate the disease of relief which is eating like a cancer into the very heart of our country, then that disease will ruin it when this present conflict is over.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it would best meet the wishes of the house if I were not to deal with the broader aspects of the problem mentioned by the hon. members for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) and Three Rivers (Mr. Ryan). I regret exceedingly that when I rose previously I did not see the hon. member for Three Rivers standing in his place; otherwise of course I would have at once accorded him the privilege of speaking, which is his due.
The debate in this instance has been instituted by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), and he has been followed by the hon, member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). The discussion has been as to whether or not the government of Canada was justified in discontinuing its direct contribution to unemployment aid. I do not intend, sir, to engage the attention of hon. members at too great length in debating that matter. The fact that we did disengage ourselves from unemployment relief placed the responsibility on the provinces and municipalities, and so far we have yet to receive one protest from those provinces or municipalities. In other words, it has been accepted.
And why not? Even the Sirois report, mentioned by the hon. member for Weyburn, states that the primary responsibility is on the provinces.
Supply-Unemployment

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not for the unemployed.
Mr. MeLARTY: Oh, yes; it so refers to all matters of welfare.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But not for employable unemployed.
Mr. MeLARTY: It suggests-we might as well have the record correct-that subject to the transfer of certain resources, it is the duty-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And you are taking those.
Mr. MeLARTY: -of the dominion to look after the employable unemployed, by way of unemployment assistance. But that is subject to a mutual arrangement which was not arrived at.
I want to make it plain that the action taken by the government was not as a result of any conference that has been held. Let me make this clear and definite-and I believe it is a point which has been accepted by the provinces. What is the reason? I't is this: The government of Canada, bearing in mind its contributions in peace time, such as the old age pensions, and its war-time contributions, is paying about $135,000,000 in connection with social service work. I believe the figure mentioned by the hon. member for Weyburn as to cost of unemployment aid is a fair one.
Let me make it clear that the millions of dollars that are being spent in our war effort, so well known to this house, must necessarily and inevitably have an effect upon the financing of the various provinces, and it certainly has. But apart from that, we are spending approximately 855,000,000 in contributing assistance to the dependents of the men who are serving in the active forces. Then we are spending over 85,000,000 in training men to equip them to carry on the industrial work of this country, and we propose to spend, and will spend, in unemployment insurance more than the amount we are eliminating in unemployment aid. In other words, I think it is fair to say that since the war started our contributions per annum in the matter of additional social assistance have been in excess of $70,000,000.
It might be a hardship, let us admit, if we cut off this aid, except for one fact, namely that there is not one single province in Canada which is placed under an additional burden by reason of this government cutting off its aid-I mean an additional burden over what it suffered.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Over
what it suffered?

Mr. MeLARTY: I will make that quite clear when I read the figures. We were contributing on a 40-40-20 basis, and there is not one province in Canada in which the grants for unemployment aid have not gone down more than the 40 per cent we cut off. In other words, when I say that no province suffered, that might be misleading, but what I meant was this: that their contribution would have to be no greater than it has been prior to the cutting off of federal aid. Naturally they suffered to the extent that we were not contributing the 40 per cent, but on the other hand they did not suffer in proportion to the contribution they had had to make theretofore.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the
dominion government cut off its relief that automatically ended the dominion government's guarantee of provincial and municipal borrowings for relief, did it not?
Mr. MeLARTY: I do not follow my hon. friend.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In Saskatchewan the provincial and municipal contributions for relief have largely been furnished through borrowing under dominion government guarantee, and that guarantee is now ended.
Mr. MeLARTY: That is another aspect which the budgetary proposals dealt with, and I should be glad to deal with that. maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Relief was cut off but the need was still there. The provincial government refused to accept the responsibility.
Mr. MeLARTY: In view of the fact that the administration of relief is within the hands of the provinces we necessarily have to accept their figures, and I assume that a provincial government will deal honestly with the figures.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That assumption is wrong.
Mr. MeLARTY: I am going to accept it because I believe they do deal honestly with the figures. In New Brunswick there is no registration because there is no direct relief.

Supply-Unemployment

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That does not say that there is no need for relief. I have stated in the house several times that the New Brunswick government automatically cut off relief in spite of the fact that there was need for relief.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I agree-or rather I should not say I agree; the statement that the leader of the opposition has made that statement is correct. I am simply stating that I cannot give the figures for New Brunswick because there is no registration in that province.

speechtext: Quite right.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Whether or not the New Brunswick government adopted the proper policy is a question that would be extraneous to this debate. But there is no registration there.
In Quebec the figure went down to 66-2 per cent; in Ontario, 65'9 per cent; in Manitoba, 40-2 per cent; in Saskatchewan, 40-7 per cent; in Alberta, 56-6 per cent, and in British Columbia, 52-2 per cent. Consequently the point I was trying to make, that no additional burden was placed upon the various provinces by the dominion government cutting off its 40 per cent contribution-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should be glad to hear the minister on that.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will deal with it right now. While the dominion is invading the provincial field, the hon. member will recall that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stated that action would be taken to stabilize the finances of the various provinces.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If they conform.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am dealing with the point raised by the hon. member for Bow River. Here is what the Minister of Finance stated:
Such payments will be augmented by appropriate fiscal-need subsidies where it can be shown that these are necessary. At the same time it is proposed to discontinue the present special grants which are voted annually by parliament.
And that is exactly what has happened. The fact that the dominion is invading the provincial field does not and cannot alter this fact, that as compensation for so invading, the dominion is willing to make substantial contributions to the provincial revenues.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Under
certain circumstances.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It must be under certain circumstances.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is a condition there.

You would not make it except under certain circumstances.
The hon. member for Weyburn made the point yesterday that employment in Canada is not being distributed equally over all the provinces. That is true; I think that must be agreed to. speechtext: I could not give the actual figures-just the percentage.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is important.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

General employment;
compiled by the bureau of statistics.

Of course, since 1926

During the depression it was a liability, undoubtedly, so far as employment went; but just now, with the manufacture of automobiles and other things speeded up, it would assist in respect to these particular figures, I believe.

I cannot reply to the
other question of the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar. I do not know. I am merely giving the figures which the bureau of statistics prepares; and after all, as the hon. member suggests, that is all I can do.
The hon. member for Weyburn mentioned a figure of $10,000,000 which, he said, had been spent on welfare. I do not know where that figure comes from.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said thirteen and a quarter million dollars.

Well, bearing in mind

Without any dominion

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have no objection to these questions. I think they are helpful.

speechtext:
There is a
discrepancy in the figures. I merely want to get them straight.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am giving the hon.
member for Weyburn the figures which were given me by my department and which are compiled by the bureau of statistics. I believe that they include all branches of contribution by the dominion government to unemployment aid.
There is another point. This, it can be urged against us, is an afterthought; namely, we decided it was wise in connection with our war effort to cut off our contribution to unemployment aid. The hon. member for Weyburn made the comparison that whereas we are expending $1,300,000,000 on war, and only about one per cent of that amount, or $13,500,000, on relief, we should not have further reduced it. If you apply that argument, sir, to all matters of expenditure, I imagine that you would have a total outlay which would outrun even the expenditure which unfortunately we have to make because of the necessities of war.
But in his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stated that he is prepared to consider and make recommendations; that if it becomes necessary to compensate the provinces by reason of the income which has been taken from them-referred to by the hon. member for Weyburn-he is prepared to give consideration to compensatory measures. If we consider that this government is saddled with the expense naturally involved in the war, if we assume that because of the economic upsurge the provincial revenues are much higher than they ever were, and if we assume that the number on welfare is so much lower that the expenditure is not going to be placed on the provinces and the municipalities, I believe this house will agree that the government has taken the proper course.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just before we leave this matter, may I suggest to the minister that before the labour estimates come down the figures might be looked into. I have here the figures which were given by the premier of Saskatchewan in his budget speech. They are as follows:
(round figures)

Total for the year	 $10,600,000

Supply-Unemployment

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no question that there is a discrepancy. I do not know what the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan had in mind, but I should be very glad to give the 'hon. member the figures. I believe that those which I have quoted are correct.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The figures I have mentioned are the budgetary figures of Saskatchewan. We will get it straightened out when the labour estimates come on.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker,-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that he has already spoken in the debate.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did his best to speak.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And my best-*

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: was not the best.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-was not good enough. I do not think I have spoken in this debate at all. In any case, I am not going to speak now in this debate-that is to say, not on this particular subject. But while we are under this order of business there is a matter to which I think the house should give some attention: I refer to the question of labour disputes and the government's attitude and policy in regard thereto.
There has been since a certain occurrence last week a considerable amount of editorial comment in some of our papers, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) indicated last Friday that he would like to have a debate on the matter. I do not intend to criticize the government in respect of the matter to which I am going to refer. In fact, strange as it may seem, I am going to do the opposite and commend it for certain things that have been done. Moreover, I am anxious that means may be found of resolving labour disputes in conformity with the high principles for which we are contending in this war.
When I tried to raise this question a week ago yesterday, you, sir, ruled against me. I am not now holding anything against Your Honour for that, considering how things have gone. Last Monday evening the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), with the concurrence and maybe on the advice of the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty). appointed a controller to take charge of the National Steel Car corporation's plant at Hamilton. I commend both ministers for this action. No sooner, however, was Mr. R. J. Magor of the National Steel Car corporation shown that he was not as powerful a fuehrer as he thought he was than he rushed
into the press with a half-page advertisement of the most scurrilous and libellous kind; and then certain newspapers, whose only reason for existence, so far as I have been able to find out, either in peace or in war, is the defence of privilege, began to urge the government to clamp down on labour.
I refer particularly to the Montreal Gazette, which, with its usual bias against organized labour and its usual disregard of the facts where there is a clash between organized labour and employers, editorially incited the government to strong-arm action against labour. Indeed, on this occasion the Montreal Gazette forgot the proper functions of a newspaper to the extent of contaminating its news report with opinions and suggestions in regard to this matter.
The Ottawa Journal also had an editorial on the subject, which in my opinion was an attempt to creat prejudice against the Congress of Industrial Organization. I was surprised that the Ottawa Journal should stoop to that kind of thing; it is not a role which is worthy of the high standard of the editorial policy of that paper.
The Ottawa Citizen also commented editorially on the question of labour disputes, in a manner which met all the requirements of the low standard to which that paper has sunk during recent years.
The Montreal Gazette, in an editorial on May 1, under the heading "No Strikes During War," has this to say, among other things:
When wages are high and employment good it is no time to be calling strikes,-
I presume the Montreal Gazette was referring to the wage of 30-7 cents per hour in the Peck Rolling Mills of Montreal as wages that are high.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is
the lowest, is it not?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend was
getting the lowest wage he would not think he was getting a high wage.
[DOT]-especially when the calling is done by a foreign labour organization-
A foreign labour organization! Looking around the house I see a number of people, including myself, who are members of "foreign labour organizations," if we wish to call them that; but I submit that we are just as good Canadians and Britishers as the editor of the Montreal Gazette.
-and to the impairment of a war effort that is vital. ... It is impossible for authorities at Ottawa to be unaware of the character and significance of the C.I.O. campaign in this country, of the danger present in that campaign. To be aware of it and to refrain from dealing with it is a dereliction of duty, and things like



Supply-Unemployment
that are not permitted in time of war where the war effort itself is concerned. It will not do for the government to step in and take control when the grievance is on one side, unless it is equally prepared to act as promptly and as forcefully when the grievance is on the other.
That is an assumption that the case of the Peck Rolling Mills and that of the National Steel Car company were on a similar basis, which is erroneous, as the editor of the Gazette could have found out for himself. Then I take the Journal of May 3. I quote:
All of us must admit that what might have been a good case for any industry or business in peace is not necessarily a good case in war. Concessions must be made; seeming injustice and wrong accepted, for* the sake of war effort. More: no one in this country should want any industry or employer to retard war production by standing at this time against the rights of unions, against collective bargaining, or against the rights of workers to select their own bargaining agency.
But that is exactly what has been done in almost every instance, finally ending in labour dispute and strike. The Journal goes on:
Above all, there can be no toleration of agitators (some of them not even Canadian citizens) who seem bent upon trouble, and who evidently have no regard-to say the least tor Canada's war position.
That, I submit, is a libellous and scurrilous attack on the labour movement in the country. Take the leaders in the trades and labour congress in Canada, affiliated with the American Federation of Labour here. Take the leaders of the Canadian Congress of Labour, people who, as far as I know, are all Canadians and in my opinion very conservative Canadians-not using that word in its political-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Objectionable.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not objectionable. I am not using it in its political sense. But certainly these people are just as patriotic, just as loyal as either the editor of the Ottawa Journal or the editor of the Montreal Gazette.
I am going to take a little time to show the difference between the situation in the National Steel Car company and in the Peck Rolling Mills. There are other strikes that these papers do not say anything about. They do not tell the people that there was a conciliation board in connection with the Canadian Seamen's union and certain ships on the great lakes; a unanimous award was made by the conciliation board and the employers have disregarded it. They do not come out and say that the employers must be made to accept these awards; that would be tramping on the toes of the employers, whom they are so anxious to protect. The next thing

we know these men will be calling the Right Hon. Ernest Bevin disloyal and a traitor! In this country he would have the greatest difficulty in rising from the ranks of the unskilled workers, which he organized and built up into a powerful trade union, himself coming to the position of second most important minister in the imperial cabinet.
The situation in regard to the National Steel Car company, as I understand it, is this. They had been for over a month trying to get a conciliation board.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Whom
does the hon. member mean by "they"? How many?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The employees, or certain employees in certain sections of the National Steel Car corporation plant.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What proportion of the employees?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a part of the whole question at issue. A conciliation board was granted. It consisted of His Honour Judge Dowler, R. R. Evans, K.C., representing the employers and J. L. Cohen, K.C., representing the employees. After the investigation had gone on for a short time the chairman, Mr. Justice Dowler, and Mr. Cohen decided that iu order that the board might carry on its work and be in a position to make a report, certain things should be done. One of the matters in dispute was that men were being dismissed because they were members of the union, and in order that that matter might be settled and that the board might find whether the employees of the company wanted to be represented by the steel workers' organization, the board made two proposals. It did not make an award; it made an interim report. The purpose of the interim report, if accepted by both sides, was that the board would then go on to investigate and conciliate the differences between the company and its employees, or else would bring the company and the employees together so that they could settle their own differences without the intervention of a third party. That is the proper way for a conciliation board to act-first to try to get the parties together in order that they may settle their own affairs amicably if possible. It is only where it is impossible to get the parties to negotiate, or where they cannot agree, that the board carries on its work and finally makes an award.
In the interim report one of the proposals was-I am reading from the report:
We have also indicated in the direction for the vote that the employees entitled to participate in such ballot, other than office or clerical employees or foremen, are as follows:

Supply-Unemploy merit
And then they enumerate the employees concerned and draft the form of ballot that is to be used when the vote is taken. I continue to read from a copy of the report:
Upon our being advised by the registrar of the result of the vote we will at once advise the parties and if, as a result thereof the right of the union to represent the employees is established, we would deem it the duty of the corporation to enter into negotiations with the union on behalf of the employees with a view, ' in accordance with the language of order in council P.C. 2685, to a collective agreement and the mutual disposition of all outstanding issues and differences. . . .
We feel, however, in respect to the specific case of George A. Tanner, president of the local union, and one of the applicants for the conciliation board, that we should at once, in view of these circumstances, make the finding and recommendation, which we now do, that Tanner should be immediately reinstated to his former employment pending-
Note the word "pending".

pending the proceedings of this board and pending any final disposition of his case, either by agreement between the parties or by recommendation of the board if we are still called upon to deal with the matter.
There you have the case. All that the board did was to ask that Tanner be provisionally reinstated. The company refused to do that. The board said: Reinstate Tanner and see if the employees want to be represented by the steel workers' organizing committee; then we will be in a position to carry on our investigation and make a final award. Possibly the final award would be that Tanner would not be reinstated, but it was necessary to make that recommendation in order to get a vote of the employees. The employees accepted that, although the ballot to be taken was much wider, covered the whole plant, which they had not contemplated when the board was applied for. That is the case in regard to the National Steel Car company.
The case of the Peck Rolling Mills is quite different. Here we had a board, the members of which were Hon. Mr. Justice Lucien Cannon, of Quebec province, L. A. Forsyth K.C., who I think is legal adviser to the company, and J. L. Cohen, K.C., of Toronto. The board made a majority and a minority report. I think it is stated in the majority award that on all matters except that of wages the board was unanimous. I am not going into the whole matter. But first, as is usually the case, the company objected that the steel workers' organizing committee did not represent the majority of the employees. The board had a vote taken, with the result that of 278 workers eligible to vote, 250 voted: 233 to be represented by the steel workers' organizing committee, and 17 against.
14873-164}
There were a number of issues in dispute: first, recognition of the union and the conclusion of a collective agreement; also wages, hours of work, overtime and holidays, adjustment of skilled and semi-skilled rates, sanitation, Christmas bonus, and possibly other matters. As I said, all these questions, except that of wages, were satisfactorily disposed of.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) drew attention to the long hours these men w^ere working. These employees were working a five-day week, but for four days they worked eleven hours, and the fifth day ten hours. It came out at the investigation that some of the men worked an enormous amount of overtime. Some of them worked as many as over four thousand hours a year; a great many of them worked over three thousand hours, and the others worked a larger number of hours than they would if they worked at the rate of nine hours a day, six days a week. When this was brought to the attention of the company they said they were not aware of the fact, that they believed the men were working the normal number of hours per day. I am also informed, though I have no absolute proof, that by a decision of a Quebec court in the matter of overtime rates, when these men worked overtime they were paid sometimes as little as for straight time, or even less. The board, however, recommended that overtime work should be paid at the proper overtime rates.
In the matter of wages, the majority report refused to grant any increase; but they did not say, and it is implicit in the report, that they did not believe an increase was necessary under the circumstances. They based their findings altogether on what they considered to be the intent of order in council P.C. 7440. I read from page 9 of the majority report:
It would appear that the government of Canada has, by the terms of P.C. 7440, for the apparent purpose of ensuring stability of wage levels and averting needless industrial disturbances, enunciated a war-time wage policy to which it directs the attention of boards such as this one. The principles which this policy incorporates are those to which this board, in our view, must adhere.
In other words the majority of the board felt that they could not go beyond what they considered to be the strict legal interpretation of order in council P.C. 7440. But I cannot believe that it was ever the intention of the Minister of Labour or of the government, when this order in council was passed, that decisions had to be worded exactly in conformity with this order. It is one thing to keep wages which are already fair and reasonable from rising unduly; it is an entirely different thing to keep depressed and deplorably low wages at such levels for the duration of the war.

It would appear that the government of Canada has, by the terms of P.C. 7440, for the apparent purpose of ensuring stability of wage levels and averting needless industrial disturbances, enunciated a war-time wage policy to which it directs the attention of boards such as this one. The report goes on:
Applying these principles, therefore, in our effort to ascertain whether the wage rate now under discussion before us is one which we must consider to be a fair and reasonable one, we proceed to a brief analysis of the facts and circumstances as disclosed in the material before us.
Then it quotes paragraph 3 of P.C. 7440, which was passed on December 16, 1940, and the report continues:
So that applying this- standard the wage rate now paid to employees of Peck Rolling Mills, Limited, would appear to be one which the board is bound by the provisions of the order in council to consider a fair and reasonable one.
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
It is not that the board would consider the rate fair and reasonable if it had any latitude in the matter, but it feels bound to consider it so because of the language of P,C. 7440. Then I quote from page 10 of the report:
This we have done and having found the present rate to be higher than that of 1926-29

It can be imagined what the rate was in 1926-29, if it was lower than the rate in 1941.
-we are, we think, bound by the order in council P.C. 7440 to consider that the rate is a fair and reasonable one, unless it falls within some exception created by the same order in council.
Turning to page 11 of the report I quote:
Applying, therefore, the standards set up in the order in council enunciating the war-time wage policy of our government, we feel ourselves bound to conclude that the wage rates in question before us are such as must be considered fair and reasonable ones.
The emphasis which in this majority report of the board is placed on the point that they are bound to consider the rates fair and reasonable because the order in council says so to me appears to be a case of protesting too much, and is proof positive to me that the rate is not fair and reasonable.
I do not wish to say any more about that. I believe I have shown that there is a wide difference between the case of the Peck Rolling Mills-and it is unfair to ask the government to take action, which I am glad it has not taken, and I hope it has no intention of taking-and the case of the National Steel Car Corporation at Hamilton.

The abstract rights which it is now conceded belong to labour, can only be said to exist in a concrete sense if collective bargaining is practised and collective agreements are concluded.
Collective agreements are not concluded until the companies and employees have a written agreement, or, for that matter, a verbal agreement, which becomes the basis for wages, hours and conditions of work, strictly adhered to by both parties, and departed from only by mutual consent. He continues:
It cannot be said too clearly that labour can no longer be regarded, if it ever was correct so to do, merely as a commodity. That is a fine statement, and I am proud to see it made by one of our justices. I should hope that some of the employers of labour, who have seen what has happened when labour organizations have been put out of existence, would take that attitude, and realize that we cannot have democracy and freedom and liberty in Canada until labour has the full right to play its part in the industry of the country, and all that pertains thereto.

speechtext:
But why were not Canadian troops in the Libyan desert, and later in Greece? There are two reasons. First, has the critic ever campaigned in north Africa? I have, and I wish to say that more than a year ago I warned the then Minister of National Defence as to troops from northern climates being sent to campaign in a country with so different a climate. We had the experience of Egypt, Gallipoli, Palestine, to go on from the last war, and that minister was not unaware of the dangers. That is one reason.
Here is the other. Where is the key position in this war so far as the free peoples of the world are concerned? That is no secret; layman and professional soldier alike know that it is Britain. These other campaigns are important, certainly, but Britain is the key. If Britain should fall we would lose the war.
Then where should Canadians stand if not ini Britain? The Canadian troops held the place of honour on many momentous occasions in the great war-the key positions at the second battle of Ypres, and in the Lens-Arras sector in the spring of 1918, when the huns made the last desperate dash for the channel ports, destroying the fifth army to the south of us and the Portuguese and reserves to the north. The French president had especially asked that Canadians be kept in that position, the Lens sector, the key to the channel ports.
I shall never forget the tense days and tenser nights of the spring of 1918 when the Canadian troops held that front, as to the north and south the German hordes poured through to the west, while valiant British-troops of all kinds and descriptions, flung into* the broken line in the attempt to stem the tide, fought a wonderful rear-guard action or fell where they fought. Every night where the Canadians stood, that salient became deeper and sharper; every night the gun flashes were farther back and behind us, until it looked as though we could not be saved from being completely cut off by the German armies. For days and nights one division alone held the whole corps front-necessarily a very thin sprinkling of men. One night word came up to the batteries that an attack was expected. The officers commanding units paraded their men to tell them how serious the situation was; remember, only one division folding a corps front, with no supporting infantry, no supporting artillery, no infantry in reserve, no artillery in reserve-Canada's
2594	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacKenzie (Neepawa)
thin line holding the gate to the channel. Those were perhaps the most tense moments in years of tenseness, with Canada 'holding the gate to the channel ports. And, Mr. Speaker, you know, and I know, and history records the fact that Canada held.
Now, with Britain and the world in peril, is it not right and proper that the sons of those men should have that honour to-day? Where else should they be? Is it not proper and a source of pride that they are in Britain on the main job rather than on any side issue? Make no mistake about it, our boys will be worthy sons of hard-fighting, resourceful and disciplined sires. That is why the majority of Canada's overseas troops are on that little island whose security is so vital to the world to-day, and whose defence is being watched with bated breath round a tensely anxious world.
Newspaper armchair fighters, members of this house, and others, may, with impunity, attack those of us, now civilians, who are doing as best we may the meagre, prosaic tasks allotted to us-not easy tasks by any means for those of us who always prefer action and despise .mere words. They may attack us, but when, that ill-informed criticism touches our boys on guard over there, a myriad of spirits of that other generation who found heroic graves at Ypres, Vimy, the Somme, Passchendaele, Amiens, and all the rest, will rise up in protest even though the living remnant remains dumb.
There is, of course, a certain amount of tension in war time, but it should not be necessarily as great here as in England. I am afraid there is more than hysteria in the criticism. On analysis it looks like almost four-fifths politics. There is no need of hysteria. Cool, purposeful people are what are needed in Canada to-day. Thank heaven this government can be credited with the minimum of behaviour which would lead to mass hysteria. That was one of the things I detested in the last war in Canada for the few months I stayed here after war was declared. But there need be no hysteria this time. It is a grim business. It is a time to keep one's head. And this government is giving the required lead. This sort of criticism is just as ill-informed, as ill-advised, as unfair, as one who has studied the whole problem, both in the great war and in this, would expect to find.
I wish to put on Hansard, for this house and the country to read and ponder, a short paragraph which describes, in the clearest terms, criticism in war time. The excerpt is from Trotter's great work on mass psychology, which should be studied at this juncture. This book, "The Instincts of the Herd in

Peace and War", has been called one of the only two significant books which grew out of the great war.
I have tried to show to how great an extent the average educated man is willing to pronounce decided judgments, all of which he believes himself to have arrived at by the exercise of pure reason, upon the innumerable complex questions of the day. Almost all of them concern highly technical matters upon none of which has he the slightest qualification to pronounce. This characteristic, always obvious enough, has naturally during the war shown the exaggeration so apt to occur in all non-rational processes at a time of general stress. .	.	. Generally the more technical a
given matter is, the more vehement and dogmatic is the counsel of the utterly uninstructed counsellor. Even when the questions involved are not especially such as can be dealt with only by the expert, the fact that the essential data are withheld from the public by the authorities renders all this amateur statecraft and generalship more than usually ridiculous.
Need we say any more, as to criticism
in war time? Go back over these newspaper editorial pages. Go back for some time over those pages, scan the pages of Hansard- perhaps .some pulpit has filled your ear at times-then go to the master author of "The Instincts of the Herd" and make your own comparison.
It is unnecessary to say to most clear-thinking Canadians that the men who are directing Canada's war effort have done more than a fair job; that this budget is just another example; that they have a killing burden to carry; and, although they are human, criticism which is fair, informed and constructive would be more welcome than kind words. I know, because, Mr. Speaker, I have tried them with just that kind.
The cause of most democratic sickness at the present time, of weakness in this parliament, and of most of our noise and confusion, is that too many people are saying too much about matters of which they know too little.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not my intention to refer to the principles of the matters mentioned in the budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I may have something to say when the items are before the house in committee. I intend at this time to introduce a new subject. I have a recollection that on several former occasions, two of them in particular, I introduced new subjects which were acted upon, and I hope the subject I am about to discuss will likewise be acted upon. A few sessions ago I made a speech on a national iron policy, and I am happy to say that that policy has been largely adopted so that at the moment in Ontario some 4,000 tons of iron ore are being mined daily. On another occasion I referred

The Budget-Mr. MacNieol
to a national flood control policy, and again I am happy to say that in Ontario the Grand river is being put under control against flood. I trust that on this occasion what I have to say will be followed by those in authority.
Before, however, commencing my subject, I wish for a moment to compliment the Minister of Finance upon his clear, concise presentation to the house. He had a difficult task to perform and he did it without trying to add anything to, or to take anything from, what the people of Canada ought to be told. I compliment him upon not trying to conceal facts. I also take this opportunity to compliment my leader (Mr. Hanson) upon the high plane to which he raised this debate when he made his remarks. In fact, since my leader has become the head of this party he has on many occasions raised debate to a high plane, and he deserves the commendation of the whole house for the invariable assistance which he has given the government and which he has induced those sitting behind him to extend to members of the administration in reaching their objectives.
On this occasion I wish to base some remarks upon an article that recently appeared in Collier's Weekly. After reading that article, one is bound to ask oneself this question: What is the future of our nearest British neighbour, the great island of Newfoundland, until recently a dominion but at present governed by a commission? The article to which I refer affords a great deal of food for thought as to what the present and perhaps the future position of our nearest British neighbour will be. After reading that article, I asked myself, as I will ask my fellow members to ask themselves after I have quoted some extracts from it: What is the position of Newfoundland going to be? (a) a dominion again within the empire? (b) a tenth province in our own confederation? (c) outside this empire, perhaps, as the article suggests, a state of the great republic to the south of us? I hope the answer is (b)-a tenth province in our own confederation.
For some thirteen hundred miles across the front of our country, across our Atlantic seaboard, Newfoundland's domain, including Labrador, stretches right across our great artery of commerce, the gulf of St. Lawrence. It is an extremely important question to Canada, what the future of Newfoundland will be. It is of great importance to Canada, particularly from the point of view of our defence; and similarly we are of importance to the defence of Newfoundland. The defences of the two countries are intertwined; one can scarcely exist without the other. Having in mind what the war has revealed, and also facts and figures which I myself compiled
after an exhaustive survey in that land, from one end to the other, covering a considerable period of time, I am of opinion that, taking everything into consideration, the time has come, and I hope now is, when the government should again consider approaching Newfoundland or, if the Newfoundland commission of government has not the power, then the British government, with a view to having the former dominion incorporated into Canada as a tenth province.
What did a great writer of Collier's, one of their main writers if not their leading writer, have 'to say in the issue of that magazine of April 12? I will quote a few sentences from an article referring to the bases which our cousins to the south are now establishing on that island:
Contrary to popular belief in America, the island is no part of Canada but a separate dominion in suspended animation.
By which the writer means that it is without popular government.
The belated defences in Newfoundland have nothing to do with that destroyer swap. Mounting guns on its headlands and demolishing fishing hamlets for airports, camp sites and marine bases was an afterthought. Our war and navy departments wanted them.
That is a revelation to most of us.
Canada, eager to have the yawning maw of the St. Lawrence stoppered, urged England to cede the land and the job to the states. And England herself, thinking of future exigencies as probably she has never thought before, granted a ninety-nine year deed of base occupation.
There is something new there. Later on, under the proper item, I will inquire whether Canada did ask Great Britain to grant bases on Newfoundland to our cousins to the south.
One after another, from Water street in St. John's-the street of the merchants-to the fishing villages they told us-
That is, those who were investigating and who wrote the article.
-that were Newfoundland permitted to vote upon it, eighty per cent of the inhabitants would ask the United States to take them over.
That is not so. I made a careful survey in Newfoundland and I can say this about Newfoundlanders; they are intensely patriotic, and if they went anywhere other than where they are, I am satisfied they could come into Canada.
The Yanks had come for ninetyrnine years. Maybe they would never leave. .Maybe presently they'd take the whole island' over, ship the commission of government back to England, build roads, start industries, set up Yankee relief, restore self-government.
Well, if Newfoundland comes into Canada as a province, our government will restore self-
The Budget-Mr. MacNicol

government on the island. Lastly, and perhaps one of the most important of the five sentences. I quote:
Out of all this comes the overwhelming sentiment for the adoption of Newfoundland by the United States, and there are plenty of Newfoundlanders, high and low, who'll predict that this is going to happen if they can help it.
I am not going to discuss the question from the point of view of the sentences I have just quoted, but state again that in my judgment if Newfoundland is to change its position the government of Canada might well interest itself in inviting it to come in as Canada's tenth province.
One might ask whether the time is propitious for the Canadian government to discuss this question with Newfoundland, for, if Newfoundland does join Canada, it will have to be of its own free will and on terms that are mutually satisfactory. Are the times propitious? In my judgment they are. I have always felt that there is no reason from the point of view of a Canadian why Newfoundland should not be a province of Canada. I have tried to survey the question from every angle, both for and against, and as a Canadian I see no insurmountable reason why Newfoundland should not be the tenth province of Canada, if Newfoundland herself is willing.
