speechtext:
their total imports of about $28,000,000, some $10,000,000 worth come from Canada, about $9,000,000 worth from the United States, $6,000,000 worth from the United Kingdom and $2,000,000 worth from other countries. Our exports to Newfoundland have had a beneficial effect, in bringing about in that country a greater knowledge of Canada than otherwise might have been the case.
There are many other affiliations between Newfoundland and Canada. If I am not mistaken, this government maintains the Bot-wood airport; at least when I was there, the airport was under construction, and since then I believe we have taken it over. In addition, Canada maintains all the larger lighthouses, at cape Race, cape Ray, Belle isle, Bauld, etc. In addition, if I am not mistaken, we also operate the ship that goes from North Sydney to Port au Basques. I may be wrong in that, but that was the information I received. Then the three great churches of the island are very closely connected with Canadian churches. Two of them, I believe, have their head organizations interlocked with Canadian churches, and I believe they also interchange ministers. Their school system, while not founded upon ours, uses books that have -much in common with those in this country. Therefore the incorporation of Newfoundland into Canada would be more or less of an easement; it would not be a revolution in any way at all.
A few moments ago the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) made some interjection which I did not quite understand, but I believe it was to the effect that the sentiment in Newfoundland is entirely against union with Canada. I made a very careful survey in that regard, but I did not come to that conclusion although during the course of my investigation I came close to being thrown off a dock at one of the outports; I will tell about that in a moment. In St. John's, ithe capital, I found many business, financial and travelled people, if not pronouncedly in favour of joining with Canada, at least willing to listen quite sympathetically to the suggestion of confederation. When I got below that class, however, I found the people to be strongly against confederation. I was told in St. John's that the outports were strongly against any suggestion of confederation. Therefore I went to the outports. I went up Conception bay, and got off at a number of small places. There was one small town in particular, however, about which I should like to tell the house. The main street of that town could not properly be called a street. I believe it might better be described as a road because, not having any municipal 
government, they scarcely have streets as we have them. They have no pavements, or anything of that kind.
While in that town I engaged in conversation with everyone I met. I observed one man coming through a gate in front of a fairly substantial house, and I accosted him, in an effort to lead up to a talk about confederation. They are an inquisitive people, and one has to give them credit for that. When I told him I had come from upper Canada he said, "What are you here for?" I thought I had better play safe, right away. He said, "This is a small, out-of-the-way place; why did you come here?" I said, "I came here to get the opinions of citizens in the outports in connection with confederation." I had been told at St. John's that opinion in the outports was decidedly against confederation. This man said, "If anyone advocates confederation here, we throw him into the bay." We were only about ten feet away from the bay at that time. The water was about fifty feet deep, so I said, "Well, my opinions in reference to confederation are not fixed. However, having heard in St. John's opinions respecting confederation, and having heard some people speak in favour of it, I wanted to get the contrary opinions down here."
I said to him, "My good friend, why are you opposed to confederation?" I shall try to repeat the conversation, so as to give the whole background of the erroneous basis of arguments against it. He said, "You see my residence, there?" I said, "Yes." He said, "I can turn the key in my door and go away for thirty years, if I want to. When I come back I can go right up to my front door and walk right in. No one could take my house, because there are no land taxes here; we have no municipal taxes. So my house is safe." I said to him, "But if you came into confederation with Canada you would have exactly the same situation. In Canada the provinces are responsible for municipal taxation. The federal government at Ottawa would not have a thing to do with it. Therefore, so far as Ottawa is concerned, your house would be just as safe whether you were in the Canadian confederation, or whether you remain as you now are, as an island dominion by yourself."
I said, "Look here, my friend; you call this a street?" He said, "Yes." I said, "That is not what I call it. Look at my boots. I am standing in mud right over my heel tops while I am talking to you." I might explain that it had rained that morning, and the road was very muddy. I continued, "You have not proper streets. What do you do at nights, when you go to the store up-town? You have no lights." He said, "I take my lantern with me." I said, "You have no street lights, and

The Budget-Mr. MctcNicol
you have no library. What do you do for schools?" "Well," he said, "we have three schools, operated by three churches." I am happy to say that their schools have given satisfactory service.
But municipal life as we know it here in Canada is wholly out in Newfoundland- except, of course, in the city of St. John's. In Corner Brook and in Grand Falls conditions are better, and I found some sentiment, particularly among what might be called the better educated and travelled people-business and otherwise-in favour of confederation. But the situation is changed to-day. They have lost their government. They have only a commission of government. Only a few days ago I had a letter from Newfoundland-and I do not wish to give the name of the writer, because I am not going to read it. It is, however, from a prominent man, and he states that sentiment has changed considerably.
I said to that man, in the outport to which I referred, just the same as I said to the people in other outports, that if Newfoundland joined Canada her living costs would be much less than they are to-day. I visited the corner store and took special note of the prices of certain household commodities. For instance, the price of corn flakes was slated as seventeen cents a box. In Canada we never pay more than two for twenty-five cents, and frequently we can buy three for the same price. Gillett's lye is sold for twenty cents a can in Newfoundland, and it can be bought for ten cents a can in Canada. And so on, all down the list. So I said to him, "If you joined Canada your cost of living would be cut in two, and you would be able to buy some of the comforts we enjoy".
Some people in Newfoundland are labouring under the erroneous impression that joining the Canadian confederation would mean heavy municipal taxation. It would not mean anything of the kind. On the contrary, in my opinion joining Canada would be greatly to their advantage. They would receive many benefits they do not now enjoy. They would have a greatly reduced cost of living, and would be in a position to have many of the household comforts which are commonplace with us.
In one other outport I talked to a number of sailors who had just returned from the north shore of the St. Lawrence, just west of Labrador. Lord knows it is bad enough on the Labrador coast, and it may be just as bad on the north shore in Quebec that far east. However, I said something to one of them, and he replied, "I go out there fishing. Here in my town we have nice stores, and so on. Up there in Canada there are thousands who are worse off than we are." He was speaking
of those fishing villages away down on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, in Quebec, and along the coast of Labrador. They have a wholly erroneous idea of what Canada really is.
Then, on the contrary there are many Newfoundlanders in my part of Canada, and a large percentage of them are in favour of confederation. There are hundreds of Newfoundlanders in my own constituency. I know their names

names like Cornick, Hibbs, Preston, Young, Yates, and so on. All those people are confederationists. They have come to Canada and have benefited. They would like to see their own, people in Newfoundland have the same advantages that we have.
Confederation with Newfoundland would enable us after the war to develop our whole economy right across the north half of this continent. The 40,000 Newfoundlanders engaged in fishing, the 2,500 in mining, the 5,000 in lumbering and the 5,000 in farming could take part in a continent-wide after-war development. The iron mines in Newfoundland are of great importance to Canada, and with their proper development our national steel production could be put on a more satisfactory basis, and one which would be beneficial both to Newfoundland and to Canada. Travel would be increased between the two parts of the country, and there would be profit for them as well as for us.
I have only a few moments to refer to the financial set-up of Newfoundland. They have a debt of about $120,000,000, of which $20,000,000 has resulted from their railways and telegraphs. These are owned by the island. If Newfoundland were to enter the Canadian confederation, both the railways and the telegraph system of the island would be incorporated with our Canadian National railways and telegraphs.
We could assume that cost, and relieve the island of that portion of their debt. The whole debt is guaranteed by England. I have not time now to deal with it in detail. If the old land were to take over the balance of $100,000,000, the island could enter the confederation free of debt. If we were to take over the debt of the telegraph and railway operations, $20,000,000, and Great Britain were to take over the remainder of the debt, the island would come in free. Then, with ordinary provincial grants, which we make to our provinces, and their own provincial revenue, they would be able to operate without incurring new debt. Under those circumstances they would need have no fear whatsoever of that great bugbear, municipal taxation, unless they want to adopt it themselves. I suggest
The Budget-Mr. MacNicol

that these points are worthy of consideration. Their fear of municipal taxation could be eliminated.
In conclusion, just look at the picture. For over four thousand miles on the north half of this continent we would have a truly majestic dominion, with the waters of the Pacific on the west and the waters of the Atlantic on the east bathing our shores. In matters of defence we would have full control, something which is very much needed for the added protection of Canada. We need have no fear about getting along well with our neighbours to the south. There would be no trouble over United States bases in Newfoundland. I am not going to discuss at the moment whether they should have them or not, but the United States is a great nation, very friendly to us, and we have got along peaceably with them through all the years along our four thousand mile border. Therefore there would be no difficulty between the United States and ourselves.
I submit this proposal to the government in the hope that they will consider approaching Newfoundland with a view of incorporating this island as a province and that they will approach the question in a spirit of magnanimity and courtesy, and by negotiation endeavour to get Newfoundland into confederation so that they will come in happily and be truly a part of ourselves. Then there could be no possibility of the import of the article from which I quoted coming to pass.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Prior to the six o'clock recess, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) took us on a delightful although imaginary journey to Newfoundland. I regret that I am unable to continue the same line of thought. I have elected to pursue a different course. It may not be as pleasant, but I believe it is necessary; it may even have reference to certain restrictions with regard to travel.
This third war budget, this alleged indication of the scope and scale of Canada's 1941 war effort, this offspring of strictly orthodox parentage, is essentially drastic but, in the main, was anticipated. I believe - that Canadians generally realize that sacrifice and inconvenience are essential to a total war effort. I believe that they also realize that the victory of democracy with its freedom, over [Mr. MacNicol.)
dictatorship with its slavery, necessitates the utmost utilization of our energies. It was hardly anticipated, however, that certain impositions which by this budget have been placed upon us would be imposed. Yet, to be fair, I must admit on the other hand that we expected certain impositions which have not been laid upon us.
Upon examination of this budget I regard its purposes as twofold: first, to curtail the normal peace-time activities of all Canadians -and the normal peace-time activities of certain classes will be curtailed, although I am not so sure that curtailment will extend to some other classes-second, to direct to the Canadian treasury sums of enormous and unprecedented magnitude. In fact the budget, as possibly was its purpose, reaches into the pockets of all classes of .the Canadian people.
I have in mind first the well-to-do. Undoubtedly it will reach into their pockets, but I do not know that it will curtail to any great degree their normal peace-time activities. So far, I have not seen much evidence in that direction.
Then there is the position of those of average means. Many Canadians in this class secured during this war 'the first regular jobs they ever had. During peace time they encountered innumerable difficulties in meeting the ordinary, everyday conditions of life.
Finally we have the poor, and with them I associate those of veiy meagre incomes. I might even have in mind the 279 married civil servants who receive $60 a month or less.
As regards the first class, the well-to-do, and the effects which the budget may have upon them, let me observe that the degree of sacrifice is not necessarily measured by the amount of money or purchasing power which the government takes away from people; what counts is the amount of money or purchasing power which is left after the government has finished with them. As I said a moment ago with regard to the well-to-do, I have not noticed any appreciable reduction in their standards of living. I believe that if hon. members will recall whait they have seen during the first year and a half of war, their observations will agree with mine, that there has not been an appreciable reduction. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Queleh) has just remarked, "No appreciable reduction in the waist-line." I agree; I could not do otherwise.
Then, as regards those of average means, it is unfortunate, but undeniably true, that there are hundreds, even thousands of young Canadians who, prior to the outbreak of hostilities in 1939, did not know what it meant to have a decent income or a steady job. Please do not misunderstand me. Moved by feelings of patriotism just as strong as

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
yours or mine, they enlisted, but not the least of their reasons for doing so, as some of them have told me, was that they were thereby enabled to provide at least the necessities of life for their wives and children. We are now, as a consequence of this budget *-and I realize that here, again, I am likely to be misunderstood-giving to them what we call a recompense for their services- although in fact it is not-while with the other hand we are taking something away from them. I do not think details in this respect are necessary, but I cannot refrain from saying that I do not like the pressure which is being put upon the men in uniform to subscribe for war savings. Here I am expressing my own personal view. Many of these men, some of them in uniform, some of them engaged in the civil service, have seen in the windows of the stores and in the factories things which go to make life worth while but which hitherto have been denied them. Now, upon securing the first regular employment they have had, they naturally wish to secure these commodities which up to the present have been beyond their reach. But we are going to deprive them of that privilege. We also realize that many of these people in the low income brackets have been making purchases on the instalment plan, and I know, too, that this budget is going to render it extremely difficult for them to meet the obligations they have assumed.
I could say more in that connection, but let me go on to those who come within the last category-the poor, including those of hopelessly inadequate means. I have in mind there the old age pensioners, and in a moment I shall have "more to say about them. I think of the widowed mother with children, in receipt of a paltry pittance to rear and educate them. We have also the blind, who receive pensions at the age of forty. It is an abomination to declare that a blind man shall reach the age of forty before being given consideration in the form of a pension. It is just as difficult for him to secure the means of livelihood at thirty as it is for him to do so at forty. We have not been generous enough in this regard; in fact we have been just the opposite.
I think also of those people between fifty and seventy who are to a very large extent unable to take advantage of the jobs which are created as a consequence of the war. Yet they are altogether too young to receive pensions. Ever so many of them are on relief. I have the statistics in this connection, although not before me. It is a rank abomination that we should say that while there are
many of these people over the age of fifty, unable to secure or to hold a job, and in receipt of relief, these relief allowances shall be definitely and drastically curtailed on this occasion, when there is on every hand ample evidence that the cost of living is rising rapidly in spite of the war-time prices and trade board and in spite of the innumerable declarations that have been made in this house about there being rigid control over fluctuations in prices. We have also soldiers, veterans of the last war, many of them incapacitated to a certain degree. They are in receipt of pensions, but pensions that are very, very meagre, and this added burden upon them will make it difficult indeed for them to get by.
Then we have the tens of thousands of farmers-I may be putting that figure a little high-[DOT]

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member who says "hear, hear," must be an urban dweller whc makes infrequent Sunday visits to the country. I feel sorry for him rather than critical. We have tens of thousands of small farmers who have to face this agricultural policy, which guarantees less than cost of production. These people, after we have pleaded for them, are further burdened with another three cent tax on gasoline consumed on the farm. This is a terrible situation, although the representatives of agricultural areas in Canada have pleaded for the farmers. We have the labour which is dependent upon the revenue the farmer is able to derive from his efforts, and then we have the small businesses in the smaller towns in the agricultural areas, depending once again upon those, mainly farmers and farm labourers, whose incomes are going to be terribly reduced, while at the same time prices of retail commodities which they require are moving steadily upward.
Upon these classes will fall the real burden of this war. Upon those who have suffered for years and years a degree of pauperism and misery will fall the burden, notwithstanding the fact that the problem of production has been solved, so that we are really able to produce far more than the needs of these small populations we have in Canada.
I believe that we entered this war-I will go so far as to say I believe that our government entered this war-with an outlook and understanding not in keeping with actual conditions as they exist. I said a moment ago I would have more to say about old age pensions. The consideration which we have given to the old in this country, not only during war time but during the peace which preceded the war, illustrates a condition of
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

disgrace abounding, and I do not believe I am emphasizing it too strongly when I say that. These old people were the pioneers of this country, who faced the wilderness and out of it brought the vast production which we see evident on every hand. With their vision, initiative, courage, sacrifice and thrift they opened the vaults of nature in Canada and revealed the untold wealth which is to be found there. They solved the problem of production years ago, to such an extent, it is said, that in Canada we are able to feed a population four or five times as large as that which we have at the present time.
Let me make this observation in passing. If we are not able or willing to give better consideration to the population we already have, I think it ill becomes us to advocate the supporting of a population four or five times greater. Out of our lakes and forests, out of our streams and mines and plains, we are unquestionably able to satisfy all the needs of a growing nation. We have here a land area of three and a half million square miles, which is equal to three times all Europe, not taking Russia into account, including the British isles; yet we have a population only one-twentieth of that of those areas.
These old people of whom I speak, many of whom are pioneers of the country, left assets far greater than the needs of this nation, but we have failed hopelessly in the question of properly rewarding them, as those who made it possible for the people of to-day to enjoy the things which we have in abundance. During the lifetime of each pioneer, he encountered situations where his earnings were inadequate to provide for his daily needs and also to arrange for an accumulation of savings. The result is that when he was confronted with certain unforeseen economic reverses, his meagre savings were depleted and he passed into the evening of life at the mercy of those to whom he had left the developed assets of this country.
During the time the pioneer was developing this dominion we also found developed in this country a certain system of acrobatics, if I may call it that, of economics and finance. There were brought into being certain mysteries of calculating and recording; we found the debit and the credit systems being evolved so far as they applied to this Canada of ours, and the mysteries of accounting and bookkeeping. What came out of it all? So far as the pioneer is concerned, the old person, this is what he has received out of it: in Canada we examine carefully into all the conditions surrounding persons who have reached seventy years of age; and after we are definitely assured that the sons and daughters cannot support them, after we are certain that there 
are no hidden relatives of some complexion or another able to provide for them, we grant them a mere pittance, a sum which we charge against any real estate which they may own, together with five per cent interest compounded annually. What do we give them? I have some figures here. The average old age pension in various parts of Canada is as follows: in the northwest territories it is $20 a month. There are only seven of them, and that is the highest paid from the Pacific to the Atlantic so far as we are concerned. For the other provinces the averages are:

Prince Edward Island-

pension is $11.28.
Ontario	 $18.53

I shall come to that in a minute. That same system of economics and finance which gives to the old people of Canada, after forcing them into a condition of pauperism, the paltry sums I have mentioned, has given to the retired judges of this country something like this, to one, $1,000 a month; to another $750 a month; to another, S666 a month, and ito another, $666 a month. There are five getting $583 a month, thirty at $416 a month, five at $500 # month, and one at $555. In other words, the lowest average old age pension received in Canada is $11.28 paid in Prince Edward Island, while the lowest judge's pension is $416 a month and there are thirty of them getting that. Someone suggested to me this afternoon that judges were lawyers and lawyers are usually politicians and so forth; hon. members can trace it back for themselves.
There are those who say that no consideration should be given to this matter at the present time; that we are at war. But Great Britain lowered her qualification age to sixty-five and increased the amount of pension during war time. The United States of America, through amendments to the social security act and through congressional enactment, are paying as much as $40 a month, allowing certain incomes for the upkeep of personal property, and paying $50 to $100 to meet doctor's bills and funeral expenses.

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
It is absolutely necessary at the present time to give further and more adequate consideration to this question, especially in view of the fact that we have in Saskatchewan an increase in the cost of retail commodities of 12 * 1 per cent, while in the other provinces the figures are:
Per cent
Quebec	 10'5
Ontario	 f'6
Nova Scotia	 15-2
New Brunswick	 12-4
Manitoba	 10'2
British Columbia	 9-1
Alberta	 9-8
This averages a little over ten per cent increase in the cost of the retail commodities which these people have to buy. In other words, in actually determining the amount of the average old age pension, one must reduce the amounts I stated by these percentages representing the increase in the retail price of commodities.
I would say, and I feel extremely keen about this, that it is a gross injustice which we are placing upon the shoulders of the people whom we call the old age pensioners. I do not see why this government cannot reduce the qualification age to sixty-five with sixty the ultimate objective, and raise that meagre pittance from .the present average level to at least S30 or $40 a month. In this way we should be actually accomplishing something m parliament.
I note that in this budget we have a further tax upon sugar. I do not know what line of reasoning was followed when the government finally determined to add to the tax upon sugar. By doing so they are reaching into every sugar bowl in Canada, while at the same time they are not reaching into every glass of whisky that may serve as a substitute in many instances for the tea or coffee which the humble folk drink. I said a while ago, and I reiterate it now, that I am definitely opposed to that tax increase on sugar. I do not know whether the government regard sugar as a non-essential essential or an essential non-essential; it has my head in a whirl. I do not believe that any adequate explanation was given for the tax increase.
I wish to place emphasis once more upon the fact that I am protesting against this added three cent tax on gasoline which is consumed on the farms. It is a very poor reward for the effort and energy and the contribution which the farmers of western Canada have offered for the prosecution of this war. I said that I think we failed to give recognition to the existing condition among this class of people when we entered upon this war.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) has asserted time and again, as I presume all members of the cabinet have asserted, that we are desirous of bringing about equality of sacrifice; but I say that, as a result of the gross inequalities which prevailed prior to the outbreak of war, the minister is just about as close to his goal to-day as he ever will be while he continues to pursue the course of action, with regard to finance, that he has pursued in the past. With the obnoxious agricultural policy which has been thrust upon us; with the inadequate pension policies to which I have already alluded; with the disregard for relief needs in this country, even yet, and with the centralization of industry in Ontario and Quebec, the minister cannot possibly get any closer to his goal than he is at the present time so long as the government continues to pursue the present policy.
We have now the imposition of a ten per cent tax on travel tickets. So far as the civilian population is concerned, I have nothing to say; but so far as the soldiers are concerned, I could not say what I think and still comply with the rules of this house. Hon. members have risen in their places here time and again in an endeavour to secure consideration for the boys in uniform in connection with the matter of travel. We first pointed out that we thought they should have free transportation. When that was refused we said we thought at least the soldiers should receive the same consideration that is shown civilian travellers with regard to special excursion rates and so forth. We in this group also suggested that we might afford pool rates; but what do we get in answer to our pleadings? We get a ten per cent tax on the cost of their transportation, and I say that is an absolute disgrace. I have had thousands of soldiers fell me what they think of this situation. I wish the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and the Minister of Finance could have walked into some of these training camps about the time the soldiers learned of this new imposition. As I said a moment ago, even if my voice were not failing I would not be able within the rules of this house adequately to describe my feelings in the matter.
My time is practically exhausted, Mr. Speaker, and in conclusion I should like to make this observation. The people of my constituency, Red Deer, are behind this war effort absolutely. We are not all satisfied with that war effort, but in any event we would rather push something with which we do not entirely agree than sit idly by. May I say, too, that in the constituency of Red Deer we have given generously of the best of our manhood. If time permitted I could mention
The Budget-Mr. Graydon

figures to illustrate that point. Suffice it to say that in my home town of Innisfail we have given approximately 260 men out of a total population of about 1,250. Our people are subscribing generously to the various war services; but on the other hand my constituents, whether Liberal, Conservative or anything else-and I represent them all in this house-are definitely opposed to the agricultural policy which has been proposed. They are also definitely opposed to this three cent excise tax on gasoline used on the farm; at least I have heard nothing to indicate the contrary. Furthermore, we are definitely opposed to this ten per cent tax on travel tickets, as it will apply to men in uniform. I should like to say also that in my travels across Canada I have made it a point to talk to many soldiers, without divulging my identity, in order better to understand what they are thinking. Each of these soldiers expressed acute dissatisfaction because of the fact that we have no proper rehabilitation programme for them when they are discharged at -the end of the war. Someone may say that there is such a programme in process of being drawn up, but, as the hon. member for Acadia said on another occasion, when the scheme has been completed probably the Minister of Finance will say that we have not the money necessary to put it into operation.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is not enough for us to say to these boys when they are. demobilized, "Thanks a lot. There is the boxcar we took you from; we shall see you when the next war breaks out." If this war lasts ten years we shall still have the resources of this country, and they will be more completely developed than they were at the time the war started. We shall have all the things necessary to make life worth while for our boys-food, clothing and shelter. The financial balance sheet of this country will declare us bankrupt. Just because we have a debt of perhaps nine or ten billion dollars, are we still going to deprive our boys of the fruits of the efforts of the Canadian people over a number of years, that is, the products of their own efforts, which guarantee economic security?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to-night I wish to take only a very brief time ito discuss the budget. In general I think the people of Canada will be in agreement on one point, namely, that the money must be raised for war purposes as well as for the ordinary conduct of government. Once they are satisfied that the money is being spent wisely and well, there will be no general disagreement with the taxation 
proposed, except where some obvious inequalities are found to exist. So far as inequalities in the incidence of taxation are concerned, I am not going to deal with all of them to-night. Rather I wish to leave them for discussion when the various items come up in committee. I rise to-night, however, because of a deep conviction which has come to me after reading one particular item in the budget. I thought perhaps I might bring my point more forcibly and emphatically to the attention of the government if at this time I dealt with that one matter only. Because of that one item upon which I am going to speak for a moment or so, I find that it is only with the greatest difficulty that I am able to vote for the budget.
While I was never convinced that it was a proper policy, the government may have had reasons for denying free transportation to the members of our armed forces in Canada. I am prepared to accept the word of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) in that regard, because in what I have to say to-night I have no desire to embarrass either the Minister of National Defence or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I am mentioning this matter only because I wish the Minister of National Defence and the government to change the item in the budget to which I am going to refer. I do not care whether or not they take all the credit themselves; I want no credit in connection with it, but I do want this one thing changed.
The men in our armed forces have enlisted for the purpose of saving the very institutions which make possible this budget and the discussion which is now proceeding. Therefore I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if it is fair that we should ask certain classes of our citizens not only to fight but to pay an extra tax while they are training for that fight, Canada desires to do the right thing by every man in uniform; I know the feeling in this dominion in that regard. If we err at all, it ought to be in the direction of dealing too generously with the men in uniform, rather than being even suspected of treating them in a niggardly fashion. To ask, as this budget does, every man in uniform to forego the right to some form of free transportation is bad enough. Personally I am not proud of Canada's stand, so far as that is concerned. But to ask them-and I wish to emphasize this point as best I can-to pay an additional tax of ten per cent on every railway or bus ticket offends my sense of justice and, I believe, offends the sense of justice of every hon. member. I ask the government to change that provision, without further delay.
I never was more serious in my life in proposing a change of government policy than I am at this time. The bargain, excursion

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
rate on a return ticket from Ottawa to Toronto for the ordinary civilian passenger is $6.25, plus ten per cent tax, making a total of $6.88. At certain times anyone can buy a ticket at that price. The return railway fare for men on active service who wish to travel from Ottawa to Toronto is $7.40, plus the ten per cent tax, or a total of $8.14. I protest with all the vigour at my command that this is a rank injustice against our fighting men, and I cannot think for one moment the government intended that it should be so.
For that reason I make this serious and earnest plea to the government, namely, that they give exemption from that tax to those passengers who are on active service, and that some arrangement may be made at least for furlough passes as well. I have nothing further to say at this time respecting the budget resolutions. I have brought this one point only to the attention of the government, and I say it will be to the credit of this parliament and the country if this change is made.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have never intruded unnecessarily on the time of the house, but to-night I should like to say a few words about that famous budget speech we heard a week ago. I would join with other hon. members in extending hearty congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon his clear, concise and courageous presentation. It was not tlie type of budget he or any other minister of finance would wish to deliver. Nevertheless it was a speech which will go down in history, and was undoubtedly the most important and far-reaching budget which up to this time has ever been delivered in Canada.
The minister has not shrunk from his colossal task. He has given us the plain, cold facts, without any sugar-coating; and in doing that, he has rendered a signal service to the Canadian people. His frankness, his earnestness, his absorbing grasp of the financial situation appealed to me most strongly. While he was speaking, I thought again, as I have thought before, of the sagacity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his genius in selecting for his cabinet men so peculiarly fitted for the performance of their respective duties.
I would congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) upon what I considered was a very fair, moderate and desirable criticism of the budget speech. I believe that his observations appealed to all hon. members in every section of the house. I believe that what I have said might apply equally to the remarks of most other hon. members who so far have spoken.
It is my intention to offer a few words of criticism of the opposition groups in the house for the delay they have caused in getting along with the business of the country. I hope what I shall say will not be considered unfair. To my mind much of that delay has been unreasonable and unnecessary. Much of it has been caused by the asking day after day of irrelevant questions, the answering of which has taken considerable time. Much of that delay has been caused by monotonous and meaningless discussion.
For these reasons I wish to speak for a very few minutes as the representative of the largest and most populous constituency in Canada;
I refer to the constituency of overburdened and long-suffering taxpayers. When I use the expression "overburdened and long-suffering", I mean exactly what I say. I greatly regret there is not time to develop that thought to-night in the way I should have liked to do. I shall take time for only one practical illustration, and- it is this:	These
sessions of parliament cost money. Yes, they cost a lot of money. Every day this house is in session unnecessarily means an added drain upon the pockets of the taxpayers. I often wish some of our taxpayers-thousands of them from all parts of Canada-could take their places in these galleries-

-and I believe they would see for themselves, and obtain a new idea as to how their money is wasted. We hear speech after speech expressing the same thought, in dreary repetition, while the taxpayers foot the bills and the Minister of Finance tries to collect the cash.
All hon. members realize that a task of colossal magnitude has been thrust upon the Minister of Finance. It is not one of his seeking. Everyone knows how unprepared Canada was a few years ago, so far as the implements of war are concerned. We know how unprepared we were for the present appalling war expenditures. That is not to be wondered at. We in this dominion are, and always have been, a peace-loving people, but in many instances the love of peace was permitted to override our better judgment. That was true also of England, of some European countries, and particularly true of Canada. All across this country in the last decade there swept a demand for disarmament. In the pulpit, on the platform and in the press that demand prevailed, until
The Budget-Mr. Matthews

one wonders to-day whether many of its * good and well-intentioned advocates were not the deluded victims of German propaganda.
Even this House of Commons was not free from the effect of that propaganda, if I may so describe it. The pages of Hansard tell us a sorry tale-speeches made in this chamber only three or four years ago, opposing most bitterly the voting of money for military expenditures. Those speeches will remain in Hansard, and will stand as a sad commentary upon the discernment of many of us.
I have been looking over Hansard for previous years, and I had first planned reading some of those quotations to-night. I do not, however, intend to do so, because I believe the speeches made at that time were made in absolute good faith, but in view of these facts I would suggest that some hon. members should be less caustic in their remarks about what they are pleased to term the inadequacy of the government's war effort.
Some of them, perhaps all of them, are educated gentlemen and will not be unfamiliar with that Shakespearian phrase, "Consistency, thou art a jewel." Yes, many people were fooled during those pre-war years; but some were not. I remember four years ago next August talking nearly the whole of one afternoon to a friend of mine who had just spent a few weeks in Germany. He was not fooled. He said: "There is not the slightest doubt in my mind that we shall be at war with Germany inside of two years," and he was right almost to an uncanny degree.
I am not offering these remarks, Mr. Speaker, in any spirit of recrimination-far from it. "To err is human; to forgive, divine." But I do wish to urge with all my might that now, when all our energy should be directed to winning the war, this pop-gun criticism, particularly from those who have themselves grievously erred, should be suspended. I honestly think that in causing so much delay in this house, some hon. members have not been playing fair with the country, or playing fair with themselves. History does not tell us how long Nero fiddled while Rome was burning, but I have come to the conclusion that there are some among us who have Nero trimmed to a standstill. In saying this, I have no thought of suggesting that all these modern Neros are to be found on one side of the house. Nevertheless, judging by the remarks of some hon. members, one would almost suppose that some of those on the other side of the house must have fallen asleep twenty years ago. Their dreams disturbed by unpleasant recollections of happenings in the last war, they are only now arising from their slumber and are incapable of realizing that this is a new and vastly different kind

of war, more expensive because a more mechanized war. The government of Canada to-day in the prosecution of this war has nothing to hide. But some hon. members on the other side have taken so much of the time of this house, groping for supposedly unsavoury deeds and finding none, as to lead one to suspect that during their slumber they had contracted an attack of political jaundice. I think it is Pope who tells us:
"All seems infected that the# infected spy,
As all looks yellow to the jaundiced eye."
If I may be permitted, I would suggest that the opposition groups in this parliament rid themselves of their fiddling Neros and dreaming Rip Van Winkles, and that they cultivate within their ranks a greater desire for helpful cooperation. But every cloud has its silver lining, and when I heard the hon. leader of the opposition state yesterday that it was not the intention of his party to move an amendment to. the budget, I thought it was a commendable gesture which enabled me to forgive the opposition for a multitude of their sins.
A few minutes ago I expressed a desire to say something on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada. The budget will mean a measure of sacrifice, either directly or indirectly, to every one of us. I believe that our people from coast to coast in studying this budget will realize as they never did before, the magnitude of our country's task. I quite agree with a speaker who in Ottawa a few days ago said that we are living in an unreal atmosphere, still enjoying the amenities of life, long since gone in the old land. Up to the present many of our people, so far as the war is concerned, do not know the meaning of the word "sacrifice." Believe me, we shall all know it before this war is over. I have seen it stated that the cost to Canada of the present war is already two million dollars more than that of the last war from its beginning up to the March offensive in 1918, and, further, that this year's budget alone is more than the Canadian total cost of the last war and six months of demobilization thereafter.

However, this other side of the question was pointed out, that whereas the taxpayer in

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
Great Britain pays only one income tax, the Canadian taxpayer, up to the present at least, has been paying income tax also to the province, and sometimes to the municipality. Moreover, in Britain there is no sales tax, and real estate taxes are lower than in Canada. It is also pointed out that Britain, according to the latest available figures, is spending approximately fifty-five per cent of her national income for war purposes alone. Canada this year will be spending over fifty per cent for war and allied purposes.
Therefore you see, Mr. Speaker, that so far as taxes are concerned, the Canadians are taking it, and will continue to take it. Our young men are taking it also. They are not inclined to shirk their duty. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is, I believe, authority for the statement that in the sixty mobilization and training camps across this country there are 175,000 young men fitting themselves for military service anywhere, and, in addition, another 10,000 in training centres for the defence of Canada. Besides those, there is the Royal Canadian Air Force, now numbering 50,000, many of whom are valiantly defending Canada in the clouds over Europe.
This is just about what we would expect. Most of us have always lived in an atmosphere of freedom, a heritage from preceding generations. These liberties, these freedoms, someone has said, were conceived in British hearts, born and bred on British soil. Alice Duer Miller expressed the thoughts of many Canadians rvhen she wrote these words, "In a world where England is finished and dead, I do not wish to live."
I have presumed to speak some words of admonition, good-natured, I trust, but none the less sincere, to our friends of the opposition groups. Now just a word of suggestion, of warning, if you will, to those on this side of the house-and again I speak in the interests of the taxpayers of Canada.
The Canadian people will raise the money. We shall raise it gladly for the security of our freedom and the safety of those we hold so dear. But the Scottish instincts I have inherited prompt me to say very plainly that we are not willing to see that money recklessly or wastefully expended. I do not believe that this has happened to any great extent, although some mistakes and some waste were unavoidable in the initial stages of such tremendous war undertakings. But now that we have caught our stride, every needless expenditure should be, and I am sure will be, ruthlessly eliminated. I venture to hope and to believe that in this regard the governmental departments will have the alert
cooperation of every officer in uniform, of every person in a position of responsibility, yes, of every citizen of this country. It is only by cooperation of that kind that the government can obtain the best results.
It is regrettable that among a certain type of people war has always developed a spirit of greed and a desire to profiteer. Canadian taxpayers will not be inclined to tolerate or to excuse any such spirit no matter from what source it may develop. In this connection every one of us should keep in mind the old maxim,-"Eternal vigilance is the price of safety."
Let it not be forgotten that this is the fight, or should be the fight, of every man and every woman in Canada-every one of them. It is in a special sense the fight of every young man and every young woman in Canada, every one of them; for, after all, it is they who will have to live their lives either in freedom or in servitude according to the outcome of this war. No men, no women, young or old, are entitled to enjoy the liberty of their country unless inspired with the determination, the enthusiasm, the love of country, to defend that liberty to the last ditch.
Mr. Speaker, I had the honour in this house in January, 1939, of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At that time I made reference to the approaching visit to Canada of their gracious majesties, the King and Queen of our beloved empire. They came two years ago. No words of mine are necessary to recall to you the marvellous impression made by that charming couple upon the people of this dominion. Ever since that visit the singing of our national anthem has to me, in some way I cannot explain, taken on a deeper meaning, a new appeal. There is no question about it-the visit of their majesties to Canada strengthened immeasurably the bonds of empire and has given to Canadians an even deeper personal interest in the prosecution of the war.
To-day I am in the happy position of making reference to another anticipated visit of paramount importance-the visit of that great man, President Roosevelt. What a thrill we all felt, what renewed confidence we all experienced when a few short weeks ago we listened to his significant declaration, "all aid short of war to Britain and closer collaboration in defence measures with Canada." That far-flung broadcast brought hope and cheer and confidence to every democratic nation in the world.
Then on Sunday last, the day before yesterday, speaking at the dedication of that immortal shrine erected to the memory of that great democrat, Woodrow Wilson, the president declared to the world that America is
The Budget-Mr. Matthews

ready to fight rather than have on American soil any violation of the principles of freedom or any violence to the American way of life. I have spoken of these two visits to Canada, so outstanding in their significance, so far-reaching in their results. How illuminating it would be if we could have the full story of the conferences leading up to those visits!
Some day the historian of the future will dwell upon those two events, emphasizing their tremendous significance in the winning of the war.
Some day that same historian will extend deserving tribute to a great Canadian who, more than anyone else, contributed to that spirit of good-will which culminated in those two eventful visits. He will place upon the pages of history the recognition of a grateful world to one of the greatest statesmen of the twentieth century, that far-seeing and unostentatious gentleman whom we are privileged to have in this trying period of world history as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of this great dominion.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon his able presentation of the war budget 'the other day. In my opinion he is a very capable minister.
I should also like to compliment the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Hanson) upon the high plane at which he kept the discussion of the budget in his address the other day.
I desire to offer one or two observations upon the budget, more especially with reference to the increasing disparity between the positions of the agricultural, the industrial and the organized labour population of this country; also, the lack of coordination among the various departments of government which are administering the present war effort.
In view of certain assurances, effective for the duration of the war, which have been given to industry and organized labour by the government of the day, I would urge first of all upon the Minister of Finance that he rebate the tax on gasoline which is used by the farmers for agricultural purposes. May I point out in this connection that it has been customary to recognize the gasoline tax as pertaining to the provinces for the building and maintenance of their highways. Notwithstanding that, in the province from which I come, the tax of seven cents a gallon has been rebated to date to the farmers in so far as their gasoline is used for agricultural purposes. I trust, therefore, that the minister will give serious consideration to the rebating to the farmers of this tax on gasoline which is used for agriculture.
As my leader stated the other day, the tax of twenty per cent on moving picture theatres 
will, in many instances, particularly in towns of less than two or three thousand population, which have not benefited by war industry, put the operators entirely out of business. Since the budget was presented, I have received many telegrams from operators in our province pointing out that the effect of the levy of twenty per cent under present agricultural conditions will certainly be to force them out of business. Without a doubt, this would be a hardship upon the rural population at this particular time.
I am astonished that, neither in the budget of last year nor in that of this year, has any increased tax been placed upon liquor, which is certainly a non-essential in so far as our war effort is concerned. By contrast, it does not seem to me that the rural population should be deprived of the educational and recreational facilities which the moving picture theatres provide for them.
As to the added tax on travelling of ten per cent, the matter has been ably discussed by previous speakers, from the point of view of the efforts which have been put forth on this side of the house to obtain reduced fares for men of the armed forces travelling in uniform. It is something beyond our comprehension that a soldier should have to pay one and a half cents a mile to travel in this country, while upon the same train, in many instances, civilians are journeying at excursion rates for one cent a mile. I am sure the minister will be considerate enough to see to it that these chaps in uniform are exempt from the ten per cent which he proposes to add to the cost of travel. The minister was thoughtful enough, following representations by hon. members on this side of the house in respect of a previous budget, to exempt members of the armed forces below the rank of warrant officer from paying national defence and income taxes, and I am sure that he will give no less consideration to the exemption of these men from the new tax on travelling.
It was disappointing to me to note, in that budget presentation, the elimination of exemptions for repairs to or the building of small homes. I well remember a speech delivered in the old laud by the late King George V, wherein he stated that the success of the British isles depended more than anything else upon the home or family life of that country, and I believe that we should do everything possible to foster at all times the building of small homes and the development of family life.
There is a great deal of extravagance in the expenditure of public money at this time. As an example, let me refer to the spending of several millions of dollars among some 17,000 persons to be employed in the taking

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Souris)
of the census, despite the fact that, if it was thought advisable to take this census at this time and under these war conditions, such an efficient organization as the Teachers' Federation of Canada had offered to do this work, even during June, at no cost to the country. Several millions might well have been saved during these times of stress and strain, but the government has seen fit to appoint census commissioners on a patronage basis throughout the dominion, and millions are to be thus spent in taking the census.
Millions are being wasted in the enlistment, training and discharge of thousands of men in the army and air force at this particular time. It has been said that this is the most difficult army in the world to get into and the easiest to get out of in these days. The fact that well over 20,000 men have already been discharged from the Canadian army is sufficient proof of extravagance and waste somewhere. May I remind the house that it cost $2,300,000 to equip these 20,000 men before they went on parade; then it cost another $3,275,000 a month to support them while in Canada, and if they were overseas the cost to support them would be increased by another thirty per cent. It costs a great deal more to equip and train air men, and yet a pilot or observer who fails for some reason or another to pass his examinations, after receiving considerable training, is discharged. In my opinion, a great many men, both in the air force and in the army, should have been transferred to some other branch of the service where they could render useful sendee after having received this amount of training, instead of being discharged, especially if they had passed anything like a proper medical examination on enlistment. Certainly this is not in keeping with the plan of selectivity in dealing with the man-power of the country, both as regards industry and in the army, which was recommended by General McNaughton on September 11, 1939.
May I refer for a moment to the Canadian Pension Act. On September 2, 1939, order in council P.C. 2491 was passed conferring all the benefits of the act upon members of the Canadian active service forces enlisted for service in the war with the German reich. The terms of the order in council conferred the benefits of the insurance principle upon all members of the forces regardless of their field of service. On May 2, 1940, a further order in council, P.C. 1971, was passed rescinding the regulations contained in P.C. 2491. It conferred the benefits of the insurance principle only on those who served in a theatre of war outside Canada. In my opinion, that is not conducive to voluntary enlistment, and I think those who offer their services, all that they have, on our behalf.
should at least be given the same consideration as the men in industry during this time in the matter of protection, not only for themselves, for those who are on service in this country, but for their dependents. In my judgment, a great deal has been done by this administration, in such matters, to discourage voluntary enlistment in the armed forces throughout the country.
I should like to discuss agriculture for a moment or two. First, may I say that there is a young man from my constituency who was farming on his own in 1940 and personally performed all the duties in producing and harvesting the crop within a township which qualified under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act for crop failure assistance. He enlisted in the air force after the harvest of 1940 and is having the work done during 1941 with his own equipment; yet, because he enlisted, the Department of Agriculture refused to pay him his acreage bonus for 1940. I should also like to point out that while the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is also Minister of War Services, on the staff, which comprises 1,061 persons, there are some thirty-four on war service staff reported as returned men or wives of men with previous war service. Is this encouraging the development of an all-out war effort? On the one hand, while another department of this government has the question of western wheat pools liability for corporation income tax before the Department of Justice for decision at this time, on the other hand we have, under the Department of Trade and Commerce, a Canadian government elevator at Port Arthur, with storage capacity of some 3,250,000 bushels, leased to the McCabe Grain company with head offices in the United States, at a rental of $51,000 a year; and at two-thirds of a cent a bushel a month for storing grain, this company is drawing $260,000 a year from the dominion government for storing wheat in an elevator owned by the dominion.
Many references were made by the Minister of Finance, when delivering his budget, to the method of procedure at Washington. When Mr. Roosevelt brought down his war appropriation bill last March, he proposed therein the spending of one dollar out of every five for assistance to the farmers of the United States. Under our war appropriation bill for $1,450,000,000 recently passed, we allocated one dollar out of every $180 to assist the farmers of Canada-quite a contrast between the two countries in the amount of assistance given to farmers. On May 3, the United States senate committee proposed a price of $1.15 a bushel for 1941 wheat on a quota basis of eighty-five per cent of parity price, which is recognized there as approximately $1.39 a

The Budget[DOT]-Mr. Ross (Souris)
bushel. What we have in Canada at this time is far from equality of sacrifice. When the price was set for the 1941 wheat crop in this country, there was a spread of approximately eight cents between May wheat in Chicago and in Winnipeg. That spread to-day for May wheat, as between Chicago and Winnipeg, is 20| cents, which is a considerable difference in favour of United States producers.
It has been pointed out by many people, and even people who supported this government in March of last year, that the government of the day has been following rather than leading public opinion since that time. Yesterday evening the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was rather apologetic over the great contrast, from the point of view of inspiring leadership, between Mr. Churchill of Great Britain and President Roosevelt of the United States, on the one hand, and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the other, although he went on to point out the great unity which now prevailed in this country. I sincerely trust that is true, although he did not explain at what cost to the all-out effort that unity l->nrl been brought about.
There is some doubt as to the great unity prevailing in all respects, apart from the fact that the people of Canada are determined to win the war whether given proper leadership or not in so doing. I was disappointed to hear a minister for whom I have great respect, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), speaking in this house on February 24 of this year, make the statement that his province was unanimously opposed to the proposal that there should be a national government.
I cannot conceive that he really meant the interpretation which we have from that statement, with respect to either himself or his province. I know that we as Canadians are much more concerned than that about an all-out war effort. He quoted the Winnipeg Free Press of March 27, 1940, on that point. Suggestions were made this afternoon that if we really wish to know the record of this government on an all-out war effort we might refer to the various editorials in the press of this country during the past year or so. I suggest to the Minister of Justice, seeing that he quoted the Winnipeg Free Press of that date, that he might read the editorials from the Winnipeg Free Press as reprinted in the Ottawa Journal of February 22, 1941, concerning both the Prime Minister and the national government. I do not intend to quote them at length, but just refer to the matter.

speechtext:
One of these editorials
states:
An impressive case for a national war government is stated by the Winnipeg Free Press. Its impressiveness is not lessened by the fact that the Free Press is the ablest journalistic champion of Mr. King's government. In its Liberalism the Free Press is the Manchester Guardian of Canada.
The Free Press' case for a war reorganization of the cabinet is stated in two articles: An Ottawa dispatch from Mr. Grant Dexter, its able press gallery correspondent, and an accompanying editorial, obviously from the pen of Mr. J. W. Dafoe.
Further on it says:
Considered in the mass, rather than in detail, the war programme seems to have suffered from a lack of coordination, an inability to identify the soft spots quickly and concentrate on remedial measures. The desperate burden of war administration is being carried by a handful of ministers, while the cabinet at large makes small contribution.
Further on it says:
. . . while the composition of the government shows so clearly that it was originally created in keeping with party customs, conventions and necessities which rightly govern in the formation of a party administration.
Then the Journal editorial goes on to say:
Asking what changes are advisable, "bearing in mind that our sole national purpose ... is to hasten efficient production of men and material for war", the Free Press urges "government reorganization" which would involve remodeling the existing system of administration and the creation of an inner war cabinet.
It goes on at some length along these lines, and concludes:
The time and tide of war waits for no man.
May I add that the people of Canada, irrespective of how they voted on March 26, 1940, are now very much concerned about strengthening this cabinet, the formation of a central war council and an all-out war effort based on equality of sacrifice at all costs.
I close by repeating the words uttered in [DOT] this house a year ago by one hon. member:
While the sweet red wine of youth is being spilt to defend all man's highest dignity, liberty and freedom, we who occupy another form of service might well spend our time building the fabric into which may be incorporated a sounder system, which will reveal a high conception of national duty.

The Budget-Mr. Gauthier
