speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though this has no particular bearing upon the budget, I must say that the rule forbidding hon. members to read their speeches seems to me wrong and likely to lower the quality of the debates. However comprehensive a speaker's learning, however deep his knowledge of the question at issue, however great his oratorical ability and his skill at improvisation, he can always by adequate preparation improve not only the marshalling of his arguments, but also-and this is not without importance-the literary quality of his presentation. How often have we not seen a brilliant extempore speech spoiled by an error which has lowered in public estimation a political man worthy of a better fate? We all know that the best speeches, the finest lectures are those which are delivered before learned societies where the author always prepares them in advance and reads them to his hearers who are thus certain that the statements made to them have been carefully studied from all their angles.
Even in this house the most important pronouncements, statements of national and international policy and budget speeches are written and read, for the greater benefit of the members and the public. When a member speaks in a language other than his own, he wishes to clothe his ideas attractively for the greater satisfaction of his audience. Even though he may use his mother tongue, he cannot introduce any bitterness into the debate, having had ample time to think over his arguments. I dare hope, Mr. Speaker, that the house will agree with the views I have just expressed quite sincerely in my introductory remarks.
I believe that the burden imposed by the budget that is now before the house is quite heavy, and the hardships it entails should be a matter of serious thought both for those who favour a moderate participation in this war and for the advocates, nay the faithful apostles of an out and out participation, or of a crippling or even ruinous war effort. In my opinion, what has been done so far is just a beginning. Sooner or later blood donors will have to come forward in an attempt to make good our losses. In the popular language, we are burning the candle at both ends.
When war was declared one fact was selfevident; on one side, all necessary preparations had been made, while on the other everything had been left undone. So long as the unprepared are unable to meet their opponents with the same weapons and on a ground of their own choice, it is useless to expect a decisive victory. That is why the democracies must make such a tremendous effort in order to be able to fight on equal 14873-165
terms. Some see in this an indisputable argument in favour of a supreme effort, and to others it suggests deep thoughts upon the
mistakes of the past and the failure to foresee the future.
The democracies have fallen into excessive materialism. Two different factors concur in convincing a nation of its military invincibility: perfect and plentiful armaments and an absolute faith in the justice of its cause. In most cases this faith degenerates into fanaticism, and this is true of the German nation. While the money powers of democracies were trafficking with Germany and supplying it with war weapons, the German military staff, through the medium of a puppet, whom popular imagination is ever inclined to endow gratuitously with merits and qualities strange to him, was awakening in the German mind the thirst for world domination and the sentiment of moral and intellectual superiority. At the same time, prompted by the democracies on the one side, and the German political men and philosophers on the other, both the body and mind of the whole nation were becoming equally prepared to accept with enthusiasm the war which might be declared against it.
The conditions attributable to the events that have followed the declaration of war, are naturally bound to incite the inhabitants of our hemisphere to look for some means of defence, not only for the present, but for the future as well. Ignoring the existence of pan-germanism and underestimating its strength would be childish. It is imperative-and the present situation of the belligerent nations proves this fact beyond all doubt-that another driving power, just as active in its preliminary work, both spiritual and material, be set in motion and acquire at least an equal striking strength so as to put a check to the existing power whose might is in its most complete development.
It is, I believe, the Americas, the countries forming this new world of ours, who have the responsibility of organizing such a power and making it invincible. We should not fear pan-Americanism any more, for it has become a necessity and cannot be brought about without the full cooperation of all the countries whose geographical position alone is a reason for being interested in the movement. I do not wish to scandalize anybody by publicly suggesting that the seat of Canada should be filled at the next meeting of the pan-American conference.
We have the unquestionable advantage of having as premier of Canada, a man whose knowledge of politics and economics is profound, who has understood the economical, geographical and strategical importance of

The Budget-Mr. Gauthier

our beautiful and vast country long before the partisans of colonialism had discovered the existence of Canada as an entity. Should the British empire survive the terrible attacks which it is now repelling with all its might, it will be indebted for this, in a large measure, to the man who has realized what a free federation of free countries really is, and understood that the strength of such a federation resides in the added might of the individual countries. Through the friendliness that he has maintained, in spite of narrow and unwarranted criticism, with a man and a country who have become, at the present moment, the surest support and possibly the only hope of the economic body that we are accustomed to call the British commonwealth, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will truly have been the organizer of the union of Anglo-Saxon races, whose blending with the French races will form the most effective coalition against German ideology.
As a true and disinterested democrat he gives all the credit for this achievement to the Canadian people by this sentence included in his statement of March 25 last. I quote:
I venture to say also that Canadians have reason to be proud of the part which Canada has had in the reconciliation of the Englishspeaking peoples, the healing of ancient wounds, and the closing of the great schism of the Anglo-Saxon race.
Whether we want it or not, the empire, should it survive the present crisis, will owe a real tribute of gratitude to the descendant of William Lyon Mackenzie, of 1837 fame.
Our budget will impose tremendous sacrifices on our Canadian people, even though they are not the culprits. They suffer and will keep on suffering because those who were masters of the situation in 1918, and who should have acted as masters, have unfortunately given ear to the large financial interests exclusively, whose activities acknowledge no boundaries, and who believe that just reparations are nothing but bedtime stories for the weak; the halting of the allied armies on the frontiers of aggressive Germany, the exemption from reparations due by the Germans to the French people (in 1871 France had paid her indemnity in full to Germany) have been the first steps in a whole series of errors, equivocations, bargainings, and financial schemes which, after 25 years, have left us in our present situation. Those who were prompted by fear that France might become too strong, have seen their wish fulfilled. We will have to put into practice principles against which we are now fighting, and do it at the right moment.
*The word "dictatorship" frightens many people. However, we shall be forced to resort

to dictatorship against evil, be it represented by the powers of darkness or by the advocates of freedom at any price. In endeavouring to protect freedom of speech, we have allowed the propagation of too many harmful political microbes.
The countries who are now attacking the democracies have been the victims of a wrongful conception of freedom. A door opened by theories such as those propounded by Marx has led to an inferno like that of the three main socialistic and communistic dictators of Europe.
Collectivism has bloomed in those countries and it has caused the complete disappearance of personal initiative and the development among the people of a state of mind which renders them incapable of thinking for themselves.
On the other hand, great financial interests have misused freedom and even in Canada the law has been far too lenient. While war means taxes for them, it also means profits, and after the close of the conflict, they shall have the duty of helping their less fortunate fellow-citizens. To prevent a recurrence of unemployment and relief, governments should require them to supply the funds necessary for the continued employment of those who will find themselves destitute on account of a decreased activity, for some years at least, in war industries. It should be possible, for example, to open new lands to settlers, thereby offering new opportunities to all trades and callings.
Governments and parliaments have sometimes been remiss in granting too extensive privileges to bodies or boards which, after all, are not answerable to the people. For example, the civil service commission holds its powers from parliament, and the latter seems to have transferred to it some of the rights conferred upon it by the electors of this country. That commission sometimes goes too far in its rules and orders related to certain sections of Canada. Here is a concrete case: One of my electors from St. Basile, a young man of marked initiative and intelligence, wishing to put his education to good use, applied for admission to examination No. 40-1141 for the position of immigration inspector at Quebec. The commission told him:
I have to advise you that the said examination is limited to persons residing in the city of Quebec or in federal electoral districts which include some part of the city of Quebec.
A young man from a rural district, whose father has given him the opportunity of acquiring an education, is thus barred from civil service positions that are available to

The Budget-Mr. Gauthier
young men living in cities. Are not the people of my constituency also paying taxes? Are they not doing their duty toward the country as well as city people? This is quite unfair to my constituents, who, like everyone else, have a right to secure an education and to obtain the positions for which they are thus qualified. I believe that such action on the part of the civil service commission is quite contrary to democratic principles and that it rather deserves condemnation in terms which are now being merely whispered lest they reach the ears of the all-powerful chairman who has made it his realm. This is more prejudicial to Canadian unity than other things perhaps more conspicuous. I know of numerous other cases of flagrant injustice committed by the same organization. I shall take them up on another occasion.
The government should not take pattern by this organization, some of whose members claim that it is more powerful than any government at Ottawa, in the matter of leaving on the land the men absolutely required to work the farms even in war time and particularly in war time.
There are at present farmers' sons who, though absolutely needed on the land, have left for military training which will last four months-and more. I have taken the liberty, as a member of parliament and as a citizen, to apply for their release which, I hope, will be granted soon. It is necessary that the land should continue to produce if we want to feed the workers of our factories who are supplying munitions to our allies. In regard to the latter, likewise we will have to be very careful if we wish to continue producing war material. It must not be forgotten that our most practical war effort lies in every species of production. I may draw upon myself angry or scandalized looks from those who, still reeling under the impact of the new taxation, still have sufficient strength to cry "conscription," but I wonder whether they would still be able to breathe were we to add to our burden that of an expeditionary force of one-half or three-quarters of a million men. Let the government not allow itself to be frightened and deterred from its policy of voluntary support, which is all the more effective because free from coercion, by those who, for some time more, will seek by their parrot cry to remain persona grata with a small group of people for whom Canada is only a holiday resort or a land to be exploited.
Let us advise these people to try to acquire the philosophic spirit of those who are not rich but who pay their taxes while saying that after all they are easier to endure than bombing.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) expressed in his budget speech the hope that the tourist industry would yield $130,000,000. I hope he is right, but I would ask him to give a little help to the minister of roads of the province of Quebec. The normal route for tourists in Quebec is the one which follows the north shore of the St. Lawrence from Montreal to Quebec. This is the Montreal-Quebec national highway, where the scenery is the most attractive. A piece of good advice will do no harm to the Quebec minister of roads, and perhaps he will convince the minister of the need to finish this highway, the worst section of which is now in the county which I have the honour to represent. I venture to hope that the intervention of the Minister of Finance will prove effective.
It was inevitable that the state of war should set the old pot of prejudice boiling. Following the elucubrations of the Gospel Witness, the magazine Lije reproduced an article in which French Canada is represented as a fifth column. Why are people so afraid of Quebec? Is Quebec not doing her duty as the other provinces are doing theirs? Are her war factories not producing like the others? Her sons are serving in the army, some of them overseas. If the French Canadians show a marked preference for the forces intended for the defence of Canada, who can blame them for thinking of her own country before other countries? Has Lord Tweedsmuir not said:
Canada is a sovereign nation and cannot take her attitude to the world docilely from Britain, or from the United States, or from anybody else. A Canadian's first loyalty is not to the British commonwealth of nations, but to Canada and her king, and those who deny this are doing a great disservice to the commonwealth.
Is it so wrong for French Canada to think like this former British governor? I know that a large number of our fellow-citizens of English or other origin share this view. They *were born in Canada or have become pure-blooded Canadians.
Those who are most prejudiced against us are those who do not know us. Why do they not visit us? We would understand them, for few among us speak only one language. Our government has just taken another step forward in the teaching of English. Is Switzerland, with her three official languages, worse off than other countries?
Nearly every summer, the convent at Sillery is visited by a group of school teachers from Ontario and other provinces, who repair there to study French. Do you think they fare the worse for this? Mr. Speaker, we have in this house a host of members of French stock coming from the other provinces.
The Budget-Mr. Gauthier

Do they not do their share equally as well as the representatives of other nationalities? Are they not an asset for our country? Let us consider what happens in this house: do you ever see the members from Quebec rising together to oppose the measures submitted for the great advantage of the western provinces or industrial Ontario? All they require is the share to which their constituents are entitled. To this end, they do not make numerous and long speeches, they do not organize mass delegations, for they are convinced that the true Canadianism inspiring the administration will reasonably and adequately work to the best advantage of the respective provinces.
For most Canadians, it would not be necessary to insist on details, but I would like this small group, who ceaselessly acts as an ever more powerful irritant to the old wound, to lose its caustic property, and become diluted by associating with those who are anxious to see sectionalism disappear. Even if I should succeed in convincing only one of them, I would be happy of such a contribution to Canadian unity. The French-Canadians of Quebec and of the other provinces of this dominion sincerely desire the unity of the whole country. We are in unison with the different nationalities of the other provinces; in common with them all we want unity in all parts of Canada. The fifth columnists are really those who try to divide the country, to create racial discord, by using the irresponsible people of whom I have spoken. Those who stir up strife in this country and between the different races are doing the work of the fifth column. An example of the same methods may be found in the history of France, and of Yugoslavia where German propaganda succeeded in dividing the Croats and the Serbians.

speechtext:
The baneful influence of spreaders of discord in the two countries I have just mentioned is well known, as well as the result of their schemings. Their role consists in preparing the ground in which they later sow the seeds of disunion.
It is not we who belong to the fifth column but rather those who want to deepen the gulf between the races.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to quote an example from Quebec. In that province there are two organizations of St. Lawrence pilots: one at Montreal, the other at Quebec. Although I cannot give their complete history, I wish, in holding them up as an example, to pay them the tribute of gratitude which they have earned.
Strikes have been breaking out occasionally throughout the country since the beginning

of the war. Happily, they have not been numerous, thanks to the prompt and effective intervention of the government.
The two organizations I have mentioned, working in complete harmony, have experienced no strikes since 1896. The strike they declared then was in protest against the refusal to grant them a charter. They obtained their charter and have had no trouble since. These Canadians of Quebec are working for the best interests of the country.
The first organization, that of Montreal, comprises 77 pilots. They cover, between Quebec and Montreal, a distance of 139 miles.
The Quebec organization comprises 60 pilots. The distance between Quebec and Father Point is 150 miles.
The average time taken by passenger liners to make the journey between Quebec and Montreal is twelve hours. Freighters take from eighteen to twenty hours and the pilot in charge has to remain on duty from fifteen to twenty hours. There is a case of a pilot having had to remain on duty during twenty-six hours between Quebec and Montreal. The ship evidently proceeded at a slow pace.
The rates charged by the corporation of Quebec pilots varies according to seasons. It is higher in the spring and the autumn than in the summer. That of the Montreal organization is $4 a foot for ocean liners and $3.50 for other ships.
The rate for the Montreal-Sorel route is $20 a trip, and for the Montreal-Three Rivers route $30 a trip. The latter rate was adjusted at the request of the board of directors of the Montreal organization when the present Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) was Minister of Transport. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate him once more on his treatment of the Quebec and Montreal pilot associations.
I mention those associations in order to show that in Quebec, as elsewhere, and as much as elsewhere, we want to do our duty, and when we work in Quebec, even though people from other parts of the country may not know it, we do so not with any hopes of reward but because it is our duty.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that the people of the province of Quebec will show that they think in terms of Canada first and foremost. You may rest assured of the firmness of Canadian unity, of dominion unity; you may rest assured that should their example be followed by other Canadians, this country shall never be divided and subversive theories shall never become implanted here, even if through devious means and unwitting tools attempts should be made to divide us.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not know until ten minutes ago

The Budget-Mr. Church
that I was to take part in this debate to-night. I am one of the few left who came into this house in 1921, of what I might call the die-hard Conservatives. Both the Conservative party and the Liberal party in the past have done a great deal for the people of this country. There have been a great many public men coming from the Toronto district to serve Canada at Ottawa, some on one side of politics and some on the other, but we respect them all in the Toronto district and in the province of Ontario, because after all is said and done, all the good and all the bad are not to be found in one party. So far, however, as I am concerned I have been a consistent Conservative, and I say that the Conservative party need never be ashamed of its record in both dominion and provincial fields.
I have always stood up for principle. I do not always follow leaders. Sometimes I do some leading myself. The principles I have supported in the past I support to-day: for example, the protective tariff, that policy which has done so much for Canada from the day of Sir John A. Macdonald down to to-day. I believe that a right application of the doctrine of protection would solve all the economic ills, in peace and war alike, of the people of this country from Prince Edward Island right out to the Pacific coast.
I have also supported the principle of the British connection and what I believe to be the principle of sound money, brought up to date. True it is that capitalism will have to clean house; there is no doubt about that at all. There is a widespread opinion even among those who formerly were conservative in financial matters that something should be done with respect to our monetary system and monetary reform, in view of the greatest war now raging that the world has ever seen.
I think too much time has been taken up in this house in the past month with party politics. The fault is not on one side only but on both sides, even among hon. gentlemen to my left. I like them and have a great deal of respect for them. I do not agree with them all. I believe they are sincere men; yet they are not above taking a little party advantage, war or no war, and we cannot blame them for that. The past month in this house has been devoted largely to party politics, whereas in my opinion we should forget all that and meet the enemy at the gate.
Who is to blame for this budget, with its colossal expenditure? Who are the people in this parliament, past and present, who are responsible for the events that have led to this huge war budget and for this heavy assessment on the people of Canada? I
answer the question by saying that those responsible are not the only "guilty" men but those in this country and elsewhere throughout the British commonwealth who supported throwing away armaments and self-defence and threw away our friends as well and urged Britain to scrap the finest army and navy and air force the world has ever seen. Britain and France at the end of the great war of 1914-18 led the world, and if they had stood together and had not disarmed we would never have had this war to-day. We would never have seen another war. Those who supported collective security in this parliament were very largely to blame for the stand of the dominions. As a leading prime minister of France since the war once said, "It is a hard thing to deal with Britain; you can never tell about her or where she stands, for there are so many people, so many dominions, which have a finger in the pie." Canada at the various Imperial conferences, instead of lining up with New Zealand and Australia, lined up with a few other representatives and ever since the last war supported a policy of neutrality, isolationism and separatism. The guilty men are in all parties who supported Geneva doctrines, separatism, the sham of collective security and the league. Collective security is only security when you have a powerful armed Britain. The principle is all right, but it requires armed force to support it. You need force for your protection and safety to maintain the liberties and freedom and civilization which you enjoy under the constitution. I define "collective security" as leaving to others what one should do himself for his security.
Cowper, in his "Task" says, "But oh the important budget ushered in-the loud laugh -the tart reply-the learning, the wisdom and the wit-I love them all."
This budget, Mr. Speaker, forsakes the whole principle of taxation that we have followed ever since confederation. The fathers of confederation decided upon three fields of jurisdiction, a dominion government, the provincial governments, and municipal governments. When I first entered this house I proposed that we should have parliamentary, constitutional, cabinet and law reform, and that there should be a reallocation of the powers conferred under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. After that motion had been discussed in two or three sessions, a committee or Rowell-Sirois commission was appointed and made its report. But no reform was instituted.
This war, however, by big-stick methods, has caused a reallocation of the taxing powers in this country. In the last war the city of
The Budget-Mr. Church

Toronto, for example, was assessed cine mill on the dollar of assessed value by the provincial government. What for? For war purposes. Yet the war under the British North America Act was not the concern of the province of Ontario. It was the responsibility of the dominion government, under militia and defence. Right in this house, two or three sessions ago, the present government proposed that the provinces be enabled to impose a duplicate sales tax. Very fortunately that was thrown out in the senate, or we would have had to pay, in every province, duplicate sales taxes on almost every article of provisions and so forth that the consumer buys. We have seen the result of all this, in overtaxation and overgovernment in this country, with one, two, and three taxing bodies imposing taxes upon the same individual. Often one person pays duplicate, and in some instances, as in British Columbia, triplicate taxation, in the form of income tax and in other directions.
In my opinion, fifty per cent of the present budget is not for war purposes at all. It relates to a whole lot of things known as "home defence," and kindred services to protect Canada's neutrality. Let me remind hon. members that home defence here in Canada is not as important as it is in the old country, where the enemy is, as it were, almost across the road, and where new mechanized methods of warfare on land, on sea, and in the air, have caused such changes. Half the budget relates to matters which are not war essentials, which are not of primary but only of secondary importance. The defence of this country is not going to be decided at Vancouver or Montreal or Quebec or Saint John or Three Rivers. It is going to be decided over there in the English Channel in the battle of Britain, in the battle of the Atlantic, in the battle of the Mediterranean. If they fail over there, it is all over for us. Nobody in America is ready for war. I pointed this out before the war broke out, upon a motion which the chairman of the war contracts committee, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), in a private bill, introduced into this house on March 31, 1939, which I opposed. What was it, and what was it for? It was merely a proposal to declare to the world that if war came, Canada was going to be neutral, and would decide herself, or that she could do nothing without parliament, and all that kind of thing, the same as the stand of Canada at the imperial conference. We have no commitments; parliament will decide when the time comes.
As I look over the budget I find very little evidence of paring of estimates or reductions

of any kind. It has been suggested that we on this side of the house should pass this budget, that we should be just "me too" men as far as the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) are concerned, to enable the minister to impose whatever taxes he and his professors and brain trust and the technical experts of his department see fit to place upon the long-suffering taxpayers of this country, with all its overgovemment, overtaxation and duplication. Very little paring of the civil estimates has been done. If the money were earmarked for real war work, nobody would object, but, as I said the other night, forty to fifty per cent of this so-called war budget will not amount to a snap of the fingers to beat Hitler in any primary theatre of war.
The people of Canada will rise to the situation if they are given proper leadership and told it is necessary to give us that security that is better than opulence. But what have we had? Expenditures on the League of Nations, on which we have now spent a little less than four and a half million dollars; useless legations the world over on all the seven seas, thinking you are a nation when you are not a nation, when you had neither any army, navy nor air force to defend your shores; the luxury of the party system; the luxury of two railway systems; the luxury of a huge stay-at-home army; the luxury of exemptions for some of the military all over Canada. We have universities in practically every capital of the dominion. I was surprised to find, according to a return made to the house last Thursday, that, of all this tax exempt university property in the various provincial capitals, hardly any buildings had been turned over to the government for the conduct of the war. Each university is listed separately. I was astonished that, even in the city of Toronto, where the air force are badly in need of better housing, the university of Toronto have provided only one or two small buildings for the use of the government: brick residence, 184 College street; basement of mining building; south basement engineering building; small rifle range in Hart house. In the last war many of the larger university of Toronto buildings were given by the various colleges to the government. What has been the result? Duplication. Camps have been built from the Atlantic to the Pacific, at a cost of ten millions of dollars; it is said that the grand total will amount, with training and equipment, to no less than twenty-five million dollars. Where is there any evidence of saving in that direction?
In addition to all this, we have fifty-six government boards in the city of Ottawa and

The Budget-Mr. Church
other places. Fifty-six separate boards have been appointed to continue till the end of the war. The House of Commons is just a forgotten agency of government, with all these boards across the country. They are like the daily arrival of a new comet; every day, it seems, some new board is appointed. I do not know how it is possible to keep track of them. I cannot keep track of them, and I have received so much duplicate information from the bureaux that the waste-paper basket is the only place for it, because the more you receive the less you know.
Just now we have a defence board of blessed memory, which is doing a lot of talking. I said it was all board and no defence. But Hitler is not going to be beaten by talk. If Hitler could have been beaten by talk he would have been conquered long ago. Further, Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire. If Canada could have beeD talked out of the British empire she would have been talked out of it long ago, right in this house, and outside it, by those who advocated the Statute of Westminster, that empire-wrecking statute, that pointless empire divider, a year before the war, and after Munich, when we did little or nothing to prevent or provide against the catastrophe and gave away our defence and bases. But Canada will not be talked out of the British empire. Canada will have to be fought out of the British empire.
I am surprised at some elements of this particular budget. The minister has copied a great deal of it from the United States. Washington seems to be the popular place from which to borrow all our financial and tariff measures. But even down at Washington the pros and cons of the lend-lease bill were discussed for three months by the United States senate. The budget presented by the treasury has to be presented by the senate to a committee known as the committee of ways and means, and they go over every article; whereas we in this house have no power at all. Our system is two hundred years old, the constitutional system whereby we cannot strike one dollar off this present budget because, if we move to strike it off, it is regarded as a vote of non-confidence in the government. That system should be changed. We should adopt the municipal system, whereby the minister and his colleagues and all parties in the house could meet others round the table and, if it was thought fit, one or two or three million dollars could be lopped off. At Washington the Secretary of the Treasury presents his estimates and budget to the senate, and every item is gone over by the committee on ways and means.
What has been the policy in the United States with respect to war expenditures?
During the great war they charged two-thirds to capital and one-third to income. That is now reversed and only one-third charged to capital. Of course they are not actually in the war; they think they are, but they are not. In Canada the principle of paying so large a share for the war out of current taxation requires some change. The minister has to raise the money by taxation or capital loans. The minister seems to forget that this generation are suffering also in flesh and blood; they have taken on their shoulders the sins of the whole human race, and they should not be called upon to stand all the costs of the great war, of the depression, and of the present war. The minister should consider the capacity of the people to pay. It is the small man who is getting hit; even the poor women who work in casual employment during the week are not spared.
In England, under the system of government over there, the budget can be discussed day by day; one Chancellor of the Exchequer five years ago, was asked to withdraw his budget and had to do so, and he had to bring in another one, when the Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain harkened to the objectors.
It is the duty of the opposition to offer constructive criticism. The fact that the Minister of Finance and his technical experts decide upon a particular form of taxation is no reason why the opposition should be a lot of me-too's and yes-men and nodders and assenters to everything proposed and done as necessary. If we do not protest before it is too late, we shall wind up with the government adopting the whole totalitarian system, and we are heading for the Marxian state.
Under this particular budget we have federal invasion of the taxation centres of the provinces and municipalities. From confederation down to 1917 income tax was the exclusive field of the municipalities, but in that year the then Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, appropriated it to federal uses. The municipalities sent representatives to Ottawa, and they were told that it would be only temporary, for the duration of the war, but that assurance was not lived up to. Then came the provinces and invaded the field also. After the war the dominion government retained its newly asserted right to income tax, and then we had a situation where people were paying municipal, federal and provincial income taxes, as in British Columbia, on the same property or income received.
This session was only a week old when I was urging upon the government the importance of taking advantage of the lease-lend bill to get back for Canada some of the
The Budget-Mr. Church

money she has had to spend on defences on the north American continent. Do not forget that for two hundred years Britain protected America's shores, and enabled that great nation to become the country it is to-day. That was the result of the protection afforded by Britain. The mother country also protected Canada's shores; and while we admire the courage of all his majesty's forces in Canada, in the army and navy and in the air force especially, I must say that all the freedom which we have enjoyed we have owed to Britain. We are just back to-day where we were in 1812-in a state of complete dependence upon the mother country for all the protection we have-because Canada has never at any time been able to protect her own shores.
The two cardinal principles of the government's defence policy are these: First, home defence, and, second, the necessity of protecting our neutrality in the event of a foreign power attacking the United States. As I said the other day, there is very little sunshine in this particular budget, though there is a lot of moonshine and a lot of eye-wash in it. It will put a damper on all public and private enterprise.
In the last two years we have been slow to see that rights with respect to the possession of private property have been gradually taken away in this country. In the old days of Macdonald and Laurier everyone in Canada owned some private property. It might be a small mill or a small store or a cow barn or a team of horses, but the individual owned it. As I say, however, we have been slow to realize how the right to the private ownership of property has been eliminated in the last few years, with the result that the Canadian people have all become proletarian. We do not realize this. As I said a few years ago, the right to possess private property is derived from nature and not from man, and the state has no right to abolish it. Its sole function is to regulate its use. One of the glories of the Victorian era was that the people kept the state; now the state keeps the people.
In believe in the principle of protection. Sir John Macdonald, speaking in Kingston on October 5, 1844, said:
It is my firm belief that the prosperity of Canada depends on its permanent connection with the mother country, and I shall resist to the utmost any attempt, from whatever quarter it may come, which may tend to weaken that union.
I am glad to see that the minister is reducing the duty between Canada and the mother country, but he should have gone further and wiped it out when the war broke out. It should have been wiped out for the

whole period of the war. The people will not be satisfied until we get a budget that achieves that desirable end, after all Britain has done for us. Everything we have of freedom and liberty we owe to the mother country.
There are many errors in this budget. It is a piece of patchwork. It is significant, not for what it contains but for what it omits. It is a generous gesture to hon. gentlemen to the left. The professors who helped to make the budget have seen to that. This is no time for politics, but I suggest that if hon. members will carefully examine the budget they will find that the whole taxing principle upon which the government is acting is wrong. The people who are paying the taxes are the people in the industrial provinces. They pay eighty per cent of the cash taxes of the dominion.
We have had ten years of reduced consumption in consequence of the depression; there has been a good deal of belt-tightening, and taxation on the little fellow is still in force. He is taxed to death. The small white-collar worker in the department store and in other walks of life is taxed beyond his capacity, as are also the more wealthy. There are too many theories being advanced. The British economist, John Maynard Keynes, has said that unless a brake is applied to consumptive buying, the war effort will be severely hampered. That may be applicable to England, but it is not true of Canada. Taxes should be levied according to ability of large and small taxpayers to pay, and after a detailed accounting has been taken. There is too much big stick and threatening. Those least able fo pay are paying most. The burden is put upon those with small fixed incomes. The government apparently is adopting the law of the jungle in encroaching upon the former exclusive field of taxation of the municipalities and the provinces. That field, as I said before, the federal government is appropriating to its own treasury.
A few years ago, in connection with this matter, I asked whether the government would give to the municipalities a share of the income tax, but they would not do it. The pay-as-you-go system is all right, but when the government can borrow money on the terms that have been suggested, for a small fraction-the minister's predecessor borrowed, he said, for two-thirds of one per cent-I submit that a larger share, at least two-thirds, should be charged to capital. I am alarmed at the small standing army of people engaged in the publicity branches of all the departments. I suppose is gives a little more of the Hollywood touch to the various departments of the public service, but it will not help to beat Hitler.

The Budget-Mr. Church
The minister the other day in his address seemed to take considerable self-satisfaction and pride in the size of the budget, probably for fear the people of Canada would think the government was doing nothing. A great deal of the budget is only secondary. The fact is that the House of Commons to-day has no control over expenditures. We cannot strike off a dollar. A civil war was fought two hundred years ago for the purpose of giving to the House of Commons control over expenditures and over the executive, and power to supervise and regulate the executive. Now that is all abolished, and the House of Commons to-day is the forgotten agency of government. The executive rule, assisted by their new henchmen of the various boards. We have no control. Consider what is going on in the various committees to which we refer matters, and you will find that they are only conducting postmortem examinations and white-wash expeditions. The money has been spent, and no one can do anything.
The visit of the king and queen in 1939 demonstrated the tremendous popularity of the monarchy and the decay of parliament. It showed the decline of the House of Commons as a result of the house assigning its duties, powers and functions to others and abrogating its own functions, powers and privileges. As Walter Bagehot said once, the House of Commons does not like positive statements.
The House of Commons does not want to be told that two and two make four, it would rather be told that two and two do not make five. The mere size of these expenditures is no guarantee of wise or capable or prudent spending. The first casualty in this war, as I see it, has been truth, and selfrespect is the first victim of neutrality. It is hard to get the truth from the radio and from the campaign of propaganda and press agents and publicity departments to which we are subjected. The government have control of the whole thing, not only of the radio but also of the large spendthrift information bureau. There is to be a further great publicity campaign which I understand is to cost nearly a million dollars a year.
The Geneva fad is tied on to it. If you ask me, this budget is making a great many thousands of people in this country believe that Canada is heading for a Marxian state and the totalitarian form. We have gone about seventy-five per cent of the way now, and it is going to lead this country sooner or later to national bankruptcy under the guise of "socialism in our time."
Another matter to which I wish to refer relates to the soldiers. I have brought it up before, but I should like for a moment to H873-166
call the attention of hon. members to the return I received the other day about the amount of money which both the railways are making as a result of the policy of having troops stationed all over this country. I have received a copy of a letter signed by three men, good soldiers, one of whom has the D.C.M. and the military medal. I have given a copy of this letter to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). These poor men landed in gaol through forging railway tickets. A motion for going into supply is, I contend, the time to get redress of grievances, especially on behalf of soldiers of this country and free fares and insurance for soldiers. These three men write me, with reference to the ticket trial for participating in the Canadian Pacific railway fracas from Petawawa military camp, and they say:
To say the least, the whole affair has been very unfair, as only the surface has been scratched, and we few used as the goat. In fact if an honest, thorough investigation had been made, many hundreds of troops would have been involved, as this practice of travelling via Canadian Pacific railway on furlough and week-end leaves has been in practice for months, prior to any of us who were convicted being transferred here.
This statement was made by one of the Canadian Pacific investigators. Even with the full cooperation of the military authorities at Petawawa, and all the evidence necessary, the C.P.R. were quite content to choose we three and drop all the other charges. . . .
The commanding officer wants these three soldiers back. They go on to say:
All those arrested, except two, were even allowed out on their own bail a week before trial. . . .
The Canadian Pacific railway were quite content to choose the three and drop the other charges, although over twenty soldiers had been apprehended. The letter continues:
The C.P.R. officials took two and three different statements from some, and had same used in court, saying misrepresentation and other underhanded evidence was presented.
These soldiers say:
This is a very poor example of "British justice". Otherwise, the C.P.R. were not very anxious to have a wholesale inquiry and all those implicated punished according to law; it was causing too much publicity and discussion in general.
We, who openly admitted our part, are not using this as a means of covering ourselves.
Those who pleaded guilty were sentenced, but those who pleaded not guilty had their statements ruled out by the trial judge as not being voluntary, so that if they had all had counsel and all had pleaded not guilty they would have got off, because these constables who laid the complaint got two or

The Budget-Mr. Church

three contradictory statements from them, which were ruled out as not a voluntary statement. The letter continues:
Since we were arrested on March 8, 1941, not one orderly officer from the camp has ever completed his duty by paying us a visit, even before we were convicted.
Also, we were denied legal representation by our training centre, although there are many officers available who are lawyers in civil life. We had to obtain our own legal representative, paid by some of our fellow soldiers, as we cannot even draw any pay coming to us while in civil custody.
A married soldier who has to assign $20 of his pay monthly to his loved ones at home, draws $19 per month, being paid on the fifteenth and thirtieth respectively.
It costs $9.40 for a return furlough ticket to Toronto, leaving him ten cents to spend; otherwise he pays the C.P.R. one-half of his earning on railway fare in twelve months to get home for one and a half days' leave to see his family and friends, being allowed one week-end pass per month.
The entertainment is very inadequate in a camp of such a size, in comparison to Borden, Toronto, London and other depots.
It costs the soldier eighty cents return, packed in taxis to go for an evening on midnight pass to Pembroke, there being no other means of travel available, as it 'is approximately twelve miles from camp.
We three, whose signatures appear in this letter to you, have been good soldiers, and our officers commanding are more than willing to accept us immediately upon our release from civil custody. Thanking you for all the uphill struggle you have waged for soldiers as you did so nobly in the last war, sir, we are making a plea, asking you to intercede on our behalf, in obtaining a remission of sentence.
I contend that these men should have been released long ago; they did not get a fair trial. They were supposed to have a lawyer. I asked the justice department and the Minister of National Defence to provide a lawyer, but they did not. I asked the attorney general of the province, but he refused, and nothing was done. That is not the way to help recruiting, and recruiting is going to be seriously interfered with unless the government adopt some other policy, and grant free fares, abolish the hitch-hiking decree, and give soldiers insurance.
Many matters have come up here; I wish to refer to one. We have heard a great many statements made in connection with the tariff here to-day, and proposals have been made by the two parties on my left. After all is said and done, I believe that the time has come when we in this country shall have to give attention to the writing on the wall in connection with the better prosecution of the war. It was said by a writer in the National Review that:
When the socialists agreed to join Mr. Churchill's government and to support the
fMr. Church.]
prosecution of the war, they made their conditions. The most important of these was that no manufacturer or other employer was to be enriched by war industry. The wage-earning class, on the other hand, might make as much as they could. Their incomes might be trebled or quadrupled, but all other workers for the national effort were forbidden to profit in any way.
The men who made this stipulation and those who yielded to it forgot that there is something more powerful than a political agreement, something which thrusts across all such arrangements and defeats them: this is human nature.
Without some immediate and visible incentive men will not work-for very long-with ardour. When a manufacturer is told that however great his skill and devotion, however long his hours, however much war material he produces, he will not have any reward, his efforts necessarily slacken. Mr. Bevin and his socialist colleagues know that this is so in regard to their manual worker clients. They expressly said: "Make as much as you can." Suppose they had asked the men to work for seventy hours a week for the same wage as for forty-eight hours, what would have happened? They knew quite well. Production would have slackened. The masters are like the men, like the men they need a stimulus, a rewrard, the fun of getting a prize. Both masters and men are patriots, both ardently desire to serve their country, but both need, if the arduous grind is to be maintained, the fillip given by gain.
I have been a consistent supporter and friend of labour ever since I entered the school board and the city council; I have been a supporter all my life of the trades union movement; I believe that labour is entitled to proper and adequate protection, but the war should have precedence over both capital and labour for full war effort. I hope the government will take the stand-it will have the unanimous support of the country- that the war	effort to	the limit takes	precedence over	politics	and all	parties,	andalso over both capital and labour. It has been said that a number of people would like to see the theories they have set forth prevail, but I believe the day is not far distant when	the two	political	parties,	thenew and the	old, will	have to	take notice
of the handwriting on the wall and give consideration to this matter. If I am the only man in the house to say it, I do not like this, and while I have respect for the hon. members to my left I do not like to see the war used by any parties here, large or small, as a way of advancing their own pet schemes and economic theories till Hitler is beaten.
Collective security is the primary cause of this war. As a principle it is all right if its supporters had told the world that its cornerstone was a powerfully armed Britain. Canada

The Budget-Mr. Roy
thought it had all eternity to prepare to fight Hitler. It has just a stay-at-home army, their energy being wasted. You cannot fight Hitler in that way. No troops from Canada can be sent from Great Britain to any other hard-pressed war area unless the high command in Britain get an order from the high command or some agency in Ottawa. Such separatism in war is fatal.
Ottawa never knows what the rest of the country is thinking. Everything is as usual in Canada, and the powers that be are always thinking of what men and munitions they will have at the end of 1941, 1942 or 1943. Ottawa, which misjudged the whole European situation for three years before the war, misjudged even more the present situation, and manpower. The national war service act, the thirty-day training and the four-months' training plan have got us nowhere. Recruiting has been on again and off again; conscription has been on again and off again. How is Britain to take the offensive anywhere without adequate man-power from Canada and the other dominions? We are far behind Australia, and I have been keenly disappointed in our war effort so far. What do the people of Canada think of the Geneva-minded men, belonging to all parties, who were responsible for the absolutely defenceless position of Canada when war came? The Department of National War Services is run by civilians, who do not know much about war. The ordnance and pay departments are filled with civilians, too, and I think the time has come when they should stop wearing uniforms. Why should these people in the civilian branches wear army uniforms and go up and down the streets of our towns and cities taking salutes from real soldiers? Why should they be eligible for pensions and other benefits, just like the men who are actually going to fight this war? When the British troops went to Greece there were only two divisions left in Libya and Egypt to carry on the war there. How can Britain take the offensive unless this government does its duty? When the war broke out we were told that conscription would never come, nor would it if the voluntary system had fair play. Well, unless this government stirs itself, conscription will come, and is coming, and be a factor, although unnecessary if we had a full government effort. We have conscription now for four months, and unless we do something we may have conscription the year round, because if Hitler comes to this country he will not recognize any political party but will treat everyone in the same way.
For these reasons, I do not think the budget goes as far as it should. We are taking away the revenue of the municipalities, and I do not know how they are going to carry on. The burden that will have to be carried by real estate will be terrific; and goodness knows real estate carries a heavy enough burden to-day.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the heavy taxes contained in the budget seem to have caused a great surprise to our population. Sacrifices exacted are assuredly very great, but they are the answer to the desire constantly expressed by both sides of this house which has always proclaimed an "all-out war effort.''
Nevertheless the analysis of new taxes brings up many points which it would be very interesting to study. I will mention only one, that relative to the reimbursement to the provinces of an equivalent sum to the income tax collected by them in 1940.
I see in this project the enforcement of which would be detrimental to provinces which do not collect this tax or a lighter one than that collected by others, a disguised attempt to enforce certain theories of the defunct Sirois commission. For the present I will not comment on it further.
At this moment when the issue of the supreme contest becomes more and more dreadful, I do think I can be of greater help to my country which has a direct interest in its ultimate result, in calling the government's attention to two elements of victory offered by Gaspe.
It is needless for me to recall that experts have said that oil would be a factor of victory. A mere reference to what is going on to-day and to Mr. Churchill's statement regarding the dangers threatening that vital point called Iraq, allows us to embrace at a glance the magnitude of oil importance.
The securing of new sources of this precious fuel is very important. I have already referred to the possibilities of oil-bearing areas in the Gaspe bay surroundings. From 1860 up to 1901, with rudimentary machinery, fifty wells have been drilled at a relatively small depth. One can read with profit and interest the records on each of these drillings and their oil output in the annual report of the "Quebec Bureau of Mines" for 1929 by Mr. William A. Sparks. Oil occurrences can be found to-day on the surface of the soil in many places over an area of 600 square miles. In his 1929 report, Mr. William Sparks writes this on page 7:
The occurrence of oil in small quantity has been fully established, with the result that the district has continued to attract attention and it must still be regarded as a possible source of oil on a commercial scale.
The Budget-Mr. Roy

And here is what we read in a recent report by the joint engineers. Doctor I. W. Jones and Mr. H. W. McGerrigle, for the year 1937 at pages 36 and 37:
There is some oil of good quality in this region, as has long been known. .	.	. The
region is recommended to the serious consideration of those in search for oil.
By reason of the imperative necessity imposed by actual events of attempting to discover new sources of oil, and, by recalling the past policy of Great Britain in investing large capital to develop oil wells in Roumania, Iraq and many other well-known countries, I deem it is the government's duty to undertake forthwith the drilling of such areas in Gaspe as are recommended by these engineers.
According to quotations I have lately received from Robert McMaster and Sons, of Onondaga, Ontario, the drilling of a 7.000 foot well-the probable oil-bearing depth- could be undertaken at a cost of $78,000. The investment of $500,000 would then permit the drilling of seven wells which could be concurrently done and completed in eight months' time to supply, thereafter, at Gaspe seaport, the navy and the air force, with oil which at that time might have become scarce elsewhere.
Since I have mentioned Gaspe seaport, may I add another remark on this subject matter? Has not the contingency of seeing the British navy moved to our shores been mentioned? The agreement between the United States and Canadian governments for a joint defence programme of the Atlantic coast, referred to Halifax as the pivot of this military scheme. May I mention here that Halifax, located as it is outside of this halfclosed natural barrier formed by Newfoundland and Cape Breton, is rather more a port of attack than a defensive one. From the defensive point of view, the Gaspe seaport located within that natural barrier is the most important in Canada. Engineers' reports which are in the department's hands will support this statement.
Besides, if it crosses to our shores, the British navy will be compelled to use this seaport as that of Halifax is too small and already too overfull to shelter it. Gaspe seaport therefore would offer a double utility: As a defensive port it would first be the pivot of our naval defence on the Atlantic; second, it would protect the St. Lawrence of which it is the key and which has no organized defences on either shores as far up as Quebec. But, what have we in this large and deep water harbour of Gaspe for the accommodation and supply of this navy? Practically no wharf, no transport or storage facilities for supply reserves.

If the experiences of "too late" given us by the European tragedy are to be of profit to us, we should hasten to take the benefit of these advantages immediately and have these oil resources and this harbour put to use.
So guided by imperative logic, the government will not only have the opportunity of adding greatly to Quebec's share in the struggle, but it will also grant our province a more equitable share of public expenditures for our war effort.
It is not here superfluous to say that Quebec is receiving an unequal treatment. The government information bureau informs us that, in March last, in the numerous war commissions appointed by the federal authority to organize and control our war effort, there were 63S English-speaking appointees and merely thirty-nine French-speaking. I could point out also a similar disproportion in the granting of munitions or supply contracts and of war industrial establishments in the country.
This disproportion is even greater in the granting of subsidies to industries in different provinces; some receive hundreds of millions to help them in their difficulties, while the Quebec industries are receiving very little, particularly the farm industry, the fisheries and the lumber industry which, this year, have to struggle against most adverse conditions.
We have had long debates in this house on the economic problems of other provinces and the needs of their population.
So far, with the exception of the hon. member for Temiscouata who was the only one to take a positive stand in expressing his own views, neither the government nor the opposition have paid the slightest attention to or care for the interest and rights of the Quebec province, in spite of my numerous appeals.
Quebec is surrounded by such a silence that we would think it is non-existent or of trifling importance. However, numerous propagandists do not forget Quebec when new sacrifices are needed and asked for. Quebec's contributions which have been so far quite remarkable in view of the limited resources of its population and the adverse political education it has received in the past, may diminish against our will if our economic structure is not receiving the same attention as is given elsewhere. During the Easter recess I had the opportunity of observing that commercial activity is declining in the province of Quebec. At Gaspe and along the shore the retail business has dropped this winter 50 per cent by comparison with the previous winter.
Many of our industries are seriously hit by war conditions. The lumber industry suffers gravely by reason of difficulties and especially the impossibility of transport. This industry

The Budget-Mr. Roy
is one of the pillars of our provincial economy. Will the government come to its rescue as it has done for the wheat growers in the west? Will it refuse its help as it has stubbornly done so far with regard to the fishermen of the Magdalen islands who are battling against the worst misery for over a year?
May I, Mr. Speaker, bring once again to the attention of parliament the fate of that population of Gaspe and Magdalen islands zone, geographically situated as it is to make the best defence against an eventual aggression by the enemies of democracy. The valuable contributions it has already made to our war effort have been stressed by me.
So far in the course of this session, parliament has approved of the expenditure of about one billion six hundred million dollars, all that for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada, and further, providing for the carrying out of any measures deemed essential to the existing state of war-a war we are told, and properly so, for the survival of justice and democracy.
To come back to the budget, if we are willing to share in the defence of democracy throughout the world, would it not be wise to worry about its preservation in our own home?
In this regard, Mr. Winston Churchill, speaking with the courage and frankness characteristic of his frequent utterances, declared recently that in the future the policy of the British government will be oriented towards the settlement of popular grievances. Is it not an urgent necessity for Canada to direct our policy in that very same way? In the light of the assaults suffered by democracy elsewhere, it is imperative for us too, if we are sincere in taking up the challenge, that we return to certain principles almost forgotten.
It is readily admitted, particularly under such conditions as prevail to-day, that all members of a democratic system have the same obligations, and compulsory military service and taxation upon everyone according to his means are proof of that. But if the said members have the same obligations, they are equally entitled to the same rights and privileges.
The people of the Gaspe and Magdalen islands constituency, suffering from the loss of certain foreign markets as a result of the war, are accepting, as everybody does, their share of the sacrifices required for the defence of Christianity, liberty and democracy. They pay taxes as far as their meagre income will permit. The islands alone have given more than 200 of their sons to the armed forces of Canada. We could hardly reproach these people with such a contribution. They are surely doing their duty.
But are they receiving from our democratic government the just treatment they deserve?
I have already told the house, Mr. Speaker, the causes of the misery afflicting those fishermen of the Magdalen islands: the non- or under-selling of fish, the absence of any industry other than that of fisheries and also the complete absence of any wood.
As I forecast in my speech of December 3, last, the scarcity that already existed during the summer and fall has been much aggravated since. Cold has come to add to the sufferings of those ill-fated who cannot get the coal needed for their comfort.
According to reports from individuals and mayors of the different municipalities, stocks in the hands of the Red Cross have not been sufficient to relieve most pressing eases. A family of ten, after a journey of fourteen miles with a dog-team, was given ninety-eight pounds of flour, ten pounds of sugar and one pound of beans to last for a month. Two family heads who didn't get a thing were near death from exposure when they were rescued. Many families had to share the same shelter because they had not the fuel to heat up their own separate dwellings.
Under present conditions, after so long and hard a struggle, there is yet a serious problem for a good many fishermen, that of equipment for the reopening of the fishing season. Will the government grant the help needed to permit them to earn their daily bread?
Before going on with my exposal, I must correct a statement made by a provincial officer, in March last. He stated that the increase in price of mackerel to $6.50 up to $7, in the latter part of the winter, was to put a happy end to the miseries of the Magdalen islands fishermen. It is neither the merchants nor the fishermen who have benefited by that increase in price, but a Jewish American merchant who bought that mackerel last fall for $3.50 and S4 a barrel and who kept that fish in storage at Halifax till he sold it with that fine profit. Hence the situation has not changed in the Magdalen islands, and all the letters I received are full of accounts of the most harrowing misery.
We have helped the victims of war and other cataclysms in practically all European countries. Why do we refuse help to our Canadian citizens whose right to receive it is first and foremost? It is true, however, we have helped a certain portion of our people who, from want or plenty, claimed itself to be in need. For instance, we voted millions of dollars for the wheat growers of the west when they suffered from drought. Well done! Again to-day, the government gives them hundreds of millions to retain their surplus. Now, considering the present year's abundance as cumbersome and detrimental, another
The Budget-Mr. Roy

$35,000,000 in the form of premiums is being offered them in order to prevent the same superfluity of wheat next year. When people in the Magdalen islands and elsewhere are starving why so great a sacrifice of money to fight this glut of the staff of life?
Permit me, Mr. Speaker, to point out another anomaly-not to use another description-also inherent in this question of wheat: With a view to solving the problem brought about by the superabundance of wheat, the government, by means of a direct taxation, forced the price of flour to go up, with the natural but false result of reducing the consumption instead of increasing it because the poor consumer is being given less for his money.
Partisanship, the canker of the democratic system, is the reason, in the case of the Magdalen islands, for the absence of any trace of humanity and generosity. If my constituents could not guess which of the two parties would win on polling day, are we to keep up a grudge against them? Such a free use of the ferula of party discipline explains why democracy has lost its primary form in many countries of the world and is being exposed here to the worst dangers.
It would be easy to do away with the misery existing in the Magdalen islands and with the remains of unemployment in Canada. An approximate sum of $300,000 would provide most urgently needed fishing harbours on the islands and the organization of new methods of preparation and marketing of fish. Out of the considerable sums asked from parliament, why can we not set aside a few millions and a little bit of our surplus wheat, to straighten out the economic conditions in the needy regions of our country?
The billions we spend in our war effort have developed industry in practically all the cities and favoured a great number of ph'-es in the country. Their people are benefiting from it to such an extent that we are already talking of a scarcity of man-power.
According to an official answer tabled on February 25, there is no war industry or factory in the Gaspe constituency. No contracts have been granted for either war materials or equipment in that county.
There is surely equality of sacrifice in our struggle for the preservation of those democratic principles which ensure our welfare and happiness. In equity the enjoyment of this welfare should also be shared on equal terms. It is important here, Mr. Speaker, not to overlook the fact that a great portion of the Canadian people do repeat freely that the present democratic methods, in recent years, have better served finance and machinery than they have the people and workers who suffer from this false state of things.

Through the hon. Minister of Fisheries, the government have already recognized the precariousness and the causes of the situation in the Magdalen islands.
In support of this, the following is from a letter by the minister dated July 31, 1940, and addressed to me. Here is what he wrote:
J'ai ete h meme de constater cet etat de choses et vos commentaires sur cette question n'ont pas manque, en outre de m'interesser. J'ajouterai que mon departement s'occupe en ce moment d'effectuer des recherches a cet egard et les dirigeants de l'Office du Poisson Sale sont a etudier la situation en vue de trou-ver eertaines mesures devant etre prises pour y remedier.
My own translation:
I have been in a position to ascertain the situation, and, moreover, your remarks on this matter did not fail to interest me.
I might add that at the moment my department is inquiring on the matter and the directors of the salt fisli^board are making a survey of the situation* in view of finding measures to be passed to straighten it out.
On another occasion, the government, through the right hon. Minister of Justice, promised to give help to the islands.
On December 3 last, the right hon. minister replied to me as follows:
With the first part of the hon. member's address I am almost completely in agreement. We sympathize with the distress of the fishermen of the county of Gaspe, and in helping them, we certainly will be happy to second the efforts of the various associations and even those of my hon. friend.
That is from Hansard, 1940, at page 703.
In spite of these promises the government continues to ignore the hardships and sufferings that grip more and more tightly these afflicted people, and apparently wants to persist in this unwillingness, if I judge by the letter from the hon. Minister of Fisheries, dated March 18, 1941, and addressed to me, which I now read:
J'ai votre lettre du 15 eourant, de meme que copie de celle que vous adressait monsieur X, comte de Gaspe, P.Q.
C'est avec regret que je vous fais part qu'il ne m'est pas possible d'acquiescer a la demande de monsieur X, puisque cette annee il n'y a pas de credits votes par le Parlement pour nous permettre de venir en aide aux pecheurs necessiteux.
Votre bien devoue,
J. E. Michaud.
My own translation:
I acknowledge receipt of yours dated March the 15th and also copy of a letter addressed to you by Mr. X, Gaspe county.
I regret to say that it is impossible for me to grant the request from Mr. X, because this year no provision has been made by parliament that would allow me to help the needy fishermen.
Yours truly,
J. E. Michaud.

Questions
After that, can I, in fairness, ask these people to consent to new sacrifices for our own welfare, when so little is done to ensure their own?
However, hoping the government will answer my appeal on behalf of the destitute fishermen of Magdalen islands, and that it will put to contribution, by organizing them, these two essential factors of defence and victory which are offered by our oil sources and the Gaspe seaport, I will abstain, for this reason, to oppose the new exigencies contained in the budget.
On motion of Mr. White the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at 11.04 p.m.
Wednesday, May 7, 1941.
